This work presents GLGExplainer, the first system to provide comprehensive explanations for GNNs by combining local explanations into Boolean logic formulas representing learned graph concepts. By being a fully differentiable architecture, GLGExplainer accurately translates local explanations into human-readable global explanations that align with ground-truth or real-world domain knowledge. The extracted formulas offer insights into model predictions, including sometimes incorrect rules, positioning GLGExplainer as a valuable tool for diagnosing learned GNNs.

Deep learning models, which include encoder-decoder architectures, are at the forefront of innovative solutions for a broad range of applications. Despite growing efforts to explain how deep learning models operate and incorporate symbolic reasoning with these models, numerous challenges persist regarding the development of effective tools for visualizing their internal workings. Encoder-decoder models, in particular, present a unique opportunity for humans to understand and edit the knowledge encoded in their model weights through visualization. To achieve this, our research investigates the creation of a bidirectional graph-based representation of specific network segments, which should seamlessly update underlying tensor representations. This novel graph-based approach is expected to give rise to new neuro-symbolic systems, marrying the strengths of encoder-decoder pattern recognition and symbolic reasoning. As a result, our approach is poised to facilitate more engaging interactions with deep learning models while also enhancing their overall performance by harnessing the synergies between learning and reasoning.

This research introduces an efficient method for predicting the hidden parameters of complex statistical models. The proposed approach builds on previous amortized simulation-based inference algorithms by generating artificial datasets and training a versatile model to forecast specific variables. Notably, the novel technique differs from earlier methods by enabling estimators to focus solely on critical properties of posterior distributions, incorporating prior knowledge and intuition. The algorithm's efficacy is demonstrated through practical examples, including stochastic volatility models, nonlinear dynamic stochastic equilibrium models, and seasonal adjustment models with changing patterns. Notably, following a preparatory phase lasting several hours, the model can generate posterior distributions for any dataset in just a few tenths of a second.

Research into Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) using speech data has resulted in the development of remarkably effective models that naturally encode a wealth of speech signal characteristics. Although it is known that these models excel in various tasks, relatively limited understanding exists regarding their performance on tasks related to prosody or their ability to incorporate prosodic information. We introduce an innovative evaluation framework, SUPERB-prosody, comprised of three prosody-specific downstream tasks and two related tasks designed to simulate specific prosody-based scenarios. We observe that SSL models outperformed baseline results in 13 out of 15 instances across the various prosody-related tasks, and additionally demonstrated strong performance on two secondary tasks, namely prosody reconstruction and forecasting future prosody patterns. Moreover, a layer-by-layer breakdown of the SSL models reveals that these speech models prove exceptionally suitable for tasks focusing on prosody.

Our initial effort involved creating an automated system utilizing cutting-edge techniques to detect bias in Bing and Google search results, and we further investigate gender bias in YouTube search results through an analysis of the narrators from the viewer's point of view. Although our top-performing model's class-wise accuracy fell short, indicating its insufficiency in automatic bias assessment, we instead use manually assigned labels to examine perceived gender bias in YouTube search results.

This update will detail the automated next-to-leading order (NLO) Standard Model
corrections for various collider processes using the multi-purpose event generator
WHIZARD. Emphasis is placed on NLO electroweak and QCD-EW mixed corrections within
the LHC framework. In addition, the discussion will cover recent developments
in incorporating electroweak corrections into lepton collider simulations and on
event generation using POWHEG matching within NLO automation.

Recent research on language models without tokenizers has demonstrated its potential in improving the transfer of languages and streamlining model development, as reported by Clark et al. and Xue et al. Nevertheless, the evaluation of such models is primarily based on task and dataset-specific accuracy with less consideration for factors like processing power consumption, computational speed, and the resilience of fine-tuned models to diverse data settings. To address this limitation, we undertake an extensive empirical analysis to compare and contrast the efficiency of token-free and token-based language models across multiple criteria. Contrary to initial expectations, the results show that models with token-based architectures might still hold an advantage over token-free alternatives in terms of lower latency and lower memory consumption. Building on these findings, we suggest that researchers working with token-free methods incorporate these critical aspects when designing and assessing new models.

The objective is to tackle the challenge of structured commonsense reasoning through generating a graph or reasoning-graph based on given natural language inputs. Current approaches using large language models involve encoding output graphs as a single list of nodes and edges. However, this serialised approach differs significantly from natural language data, hindering accurate predictions by the models. We demonstrate that transforming structured commonsense reasoning into a code generation task enables pre-trained code language models to excel in these tasks compared to natural language models, including when the task is unrelated to source code. Across three tasks, we observe that a code generation model performs better than models specifically fine-tuned for these tasks or even a powerful language model such as GPT-3, in a few-shot setting.

Given a subset A of an abelian group G, with a specified size, a doubling factor κ, and a small parameter s relative to A's size, this study investigates the guaranteed maximum size of a sumset A+A', given a smaller subset A' within A, with a size limit of at most s. We demonstrate the existence of a suitable subset A' within A that ensures the sumset's size is at least Ω(min(κ^(1/3),s) times A's size), revealing the possibility of a larger sumset than initially estimated. Further developing these ideas, we provide a resolution to Bollob\'as, Leader, and Tiba's conjecture concerning subsets in ℤp, demonstrating the efficacy of merely three elements in ensuring |A+{b1,b2,b3}| ≥ |A|+|B|-1 for specific subsets A,B. We further explore implications when allowing for more expansive subset selections A', including cases where A's doubling is constrained and when subsets may not be perfectly saturable with a small A'.

For dense predictions, having both high-resolution and advanced semantic representation is crucial. Surprisingly, studies show that low-resolution feature maps often produce better semantic representation, yet struggle with local details. On the other hand, high-resolution feature maps excel at capturing fine-grained information but tend to have weaker semantic representation. To bridge this gap, recent frameworks like HRNet have employed a dual-parallel strategy to share information across resolutions. We argue, however, that the lowest-resolution feature map typically harbors the strongest semantic information and needs more layers to integrate high-resolution information. Meanwhile, processing high-resolution feature maps is computationally costly, so excessive layering is unnecessary. To address this, we propose the U-shaped High-Resolution Network (U-HRNet), which prioritizes additional layers for the lowest-resolution feature map and allows for sequential processing. By realigning calculations and focusing on low-resolution feature maps, U-HRNet delivers enhanced semantic representation with no significant increase in computational cost. We demonstrate its effectiveness by integrating it with HRNet as a backbone and achieving superior results on various segmentation and depth prediction tasks under identical training and inference settings. Our implementation is publicly available on PaddleSeg.

Rapid prototyping and biofabrication rely heavily on the goal of rapidly creating 3D structures in a single step, bypassing the slow conventional methods that often damage biological cells through mechanical or chemical stress. Our method involves one-shot assembly of three-dimensional shapes through the combination of multiple holographic fields, resulting in contactless processing that works on microparticles, hydrogel beads and biological cells alike within standard laboratory equipment. Following formation, the structure can be stabilized by solidifying the surrounding environment. Unlike past approaches, this method can successfully work with materials having positive acoustic properties, doesn't necessitate opposing acoustic waves, supporting structures, or external scaffolds. Potential applications for this technology are vast in the areas of tissue engineering and 3D manufacturing.

The automation of medical evidence collection and diagnosis has become a focus of attention to ease the burden of doctors and increase access to healthcare. However, most proposed machine learning approaches solely focus on improving pathology prediction accuracy, a goal deemed insufficient for achieving doctors' trust and acceptance. In their initial patient interactions, doctors generate a list of possible diseases based on collected evidence, rather than solely focusing on diagnosing a specific condition. They explore and rule out severe pathologies first, particularly in urgent care situations, requiring transparency on evidence-based decision-making. To foster trust, a system must mimic the doctor's reasoning through interactions, including generating a list of possible diagnoses and prioritizing severe pathologies. Our proposed deep reinforcement learning framework models these aspects of doctor reasoning. This approach prioritizes interaction quality and pathology prediction, performing better than existing models.

In drug discovery, determining how soluble a substance is in water has a major impact on its ability to be absorbed by the body and used effectively in research. Researchers have turned to computer-based models to predict a compound's solubility in advance, especially in the early stages of identifying new potential treatments. This 'in silico' approach has proven useful for quickly screening thousands of possibilities and fine-tuning the best options. But standard computer-based models rely on complex mathematical theories that require an enormous amount of processing power, making them unsuitable for widespread use. Alternatively, machine learning models have become popular, but these also face problems, such as the tendency to make incorrect predictions when the data available is limited, and an inability to explain the reasoning behind its decisions. To overcome these issues, our research group has developed a new model using graph neural networks that incorporates a special technique allowing us to better interpret and evaluate the results, making the process more efficient and useful for designing effective new medicines. This model can not only provide precise and trustworthy predictions of a compound's solubility but also help identify the key factors influencing this property. This ability will enable us to make more informed decisions during the development of new drugs.

Galaxy haloes may be composed largely of dark matter particles. Their interactions could generate high-energy cosmic-rays, an indirect signature, primarily in the form of annihilating or decaying. This presentation centers around rare antimatter components, detection of which is relatively straightforward due to their scarcity. I will first summarize the diffusion of high-energy particles within galaxies and then examine the anomalies associated with positrons, antiprotons, and anti-nuclei, including a notable current interest in the antiproton excess which dissolves under rigorous consideration of theoretical inaccuracies and errors in data.

We aim to create a method to stabilize the calibration score, a metric that assesses a forecaster's quality, by averaging nearby predictions. Our results demonstrate that deterministic methods can guarantee this improved calibration, even if forecasters leak their predictions ahead of time, a scenario in which regular calibration cannot be assured. Our approach has additional benefits: it allows for limited memory recall, is consistent over time, and all predictions can be found on a predefined scale. We also tackle the associated concepts of online linear regression and weak calibration. Our study reveals that using smooth calibration leads to predictable behavior in multiplayer games called "smooth calibrated learning," in which players consistently play near-optimal strategies most of the time, a marked improvement over the results from calibrated learning, which relies on the original calibration method and only achieves correlated equilibrium strategies on average.

Multi-robot pathfinding, or MRMP, is a challenge that involves plotting safe
routes for groups of robots in vast, continuous spaces without causing them
to collide. The complexity of MRMP grows significantly with each additional
robot due to the elevated risk of inter-robot collisions. Situations are
particularly problematic in confined settings, such as warehouses, where narrow
aisles make navigation especially challenging. In scenarios involving single
robots, certain planning strategies that consider topological relationships
have proven to enhance efficiency. Our approach applies this topological insight
to multi-robot teams by introducing an analogous concept to the combined space
that they share. By leveraging our method, we show the capability to quickly
generate paths through intricate, constrained environments. Our method scales
significantly better, enabling it to accommodate robot teams that are up to five
times larger than comparable methods, and also yields higher quality solutions
that better adhere to the space's structure, compared to other planning
approaches.

This research introduces a novel approach known as Local Macroscopic Conservative (LoMaC), combining it with the discontinuous Galerkin (DG) method for the efficient simulation of the Vlasov-Poisson (VP) system in both physical and phase spaces. A key property of LoMaC is the local preservation of macroscopic quantities, such as mass, momentum, and energy. Our proposed algorithm, LoMaC low rank tensor method with DG, builds upon previous work and utilizes the advantages of DG, including its compactness, flexibility in handling boundary conditions, and improved accuracy in the long term. By incorporating the nodal DG method into the algorithm, it can handle high-dimensional problems and be extended to various types of discretizations, such as spectral methods. A series of extensive numerical tests demonstrates the efficacy of our proposed method.

In this study, researchers employ Dungeons and Dragons as a complex challenge to develop and test advanced dialogue systems. The project frames D&D as a multifaceted task for dialogue systems to both predict the game's current state based on dialogue history and create the subsequent conversational turn. To achieve this, a substantial dataset of nearly 900 games with 7,000 players, 800,000 conversational turns, and 58 million words is compiled. The dataset is enriched with automated annotations containing partial information about gameplay progress. A large language model is trained to predict the game's next conversational turn, leveraging various information inputs and generating output from either a character's perspective or that of the game's referee, known as the Dungeon Master. The model is tasked with creating either in-character dialogue within the game's fictional world or out-of-character comments discussing game mechanics and strategy. The study's outcome includes a human assessment to determine the factors contributing to the generated output's coherence and engagement, as well as an automated evaluation examining the model's ability to accurately forecast the game's state based on dialogue history and the effectiveness of state tracking in generating plausible dialogue.

A novel particle tracking velocimetry system is introduced, designed to capture three-dimensional trajectories of particles in vast snowfall-affected areas, extending several meters across, throughout winter seasons. Research using this system was conducted in the 2021/2022 winter months to study the physical movement patterns of snow particles under atmospheric conditions, with initial results presented here. Our approach employs a drone-based calibration method and showcases the effectiveness of the system by analyzing data from a selected set, illustrating its capacity for examining complex particle motion in wind-borne systems. Equipped to withstand snowfall challenges, a custom-built, modular camera setup facilitates field testing, utilizing a drone's synchronized image capture to calibrate and focus measurements 10 meters above ground within a precise 4x4x6 cubic meter space. Subsequently, we explore 3D trajectory statistics, acceleration rates, and particle clustering behaviors through Voronoi analysis based on particle path data. Moreover, we address system constraints and potential enhancements to adapt this system to various inertial particle applications.

This study introduces a new operator called the mean resolvent $\mathbf{R}_0$ that applies to the analysis and control of fluctuating flows in a stable state far removed from steady state conditions. The $\mathbf{R}_0$ operator predicts the optimal linear response of a flow to perturbation, providing a frequency domain representation of input-output dynamics. Theoretical work focuses on the periodic scenario where it is demonstrated that the operator's poles correspond to the system's Floquet exponents, including imaginary roots that align with multiples of the fundamental frequency. Normally, to determine the transfer function from input to output, numerous instances of input must be averaged over; yet for specific harmonic forces, this transfer function may be derived directly without averaging, based on a concept referred to as 'dynamic linearity.' In flows with weak unsteadiness, where external influences on the periodic Jacobian's unstable component are minimal, $\mathbf{R}_{0}$ is accurately approximated by the known resolvent $\mathbf{R}_{\overline{\mathbf{U}}}$, based on the steady state conditions. Although this theory is limited to quasiperiodic flows, the definition of the operator remains valid for a range of more complex systems, including those with continuous or mixed spectra. Supporting numerical data illustrate a close relationship between $\mathbf{R}_0$ and $\mathbf{R}_{\overline{\mathbf{U}}}$ for specific incompressible flow scenarios.

Forecast accuracy is confirmed when predicted frequencies are consistent with actual outcomes.
To create an optimal forecast, a'safety net' is devised, ensuring the forecast's track record will only improve over time.
These results stem from a single fundamental argument applied differently according to the hedging method used: either static, deterministic or more dynamic, adaptable techniques.
The discussion also includes refined definitions, insights into strategic decision-making processes and a streamlined method for making calibrated predictions about binary events.

A recent Letter by Rusciano et al. in Phys. Rev. Lett. examined particle displacements in two-dimensional glass-formers, concluding that the distribution is non-Gaussian during Fickian diffusion. We argue, however, that the varied length and time scales mentioned are already understood or poorly defined, rendering the conclusions about Fickian non-Gaussian diffusion in glass-formers and the related implications on dynamic heterogeneity questionable.

When studying the configurations of a linear polymer in a solvent, we also consider the scenario in which it forms a double polymer. Following a standard method to create a field theory based on a symmetric $O\left(n\right)$ spin model, we derive a model representing RNA or DNA with consistent monomer binding energies. This model exhibits a stable fixed point where the double polymer separates from the single-strand polymer, resulting in a conventional branched polymer with a three-point interaction, achieved through adjustment of at least one parameter. At this fixed point, with a critical dimension of eight, we observe the reproduction of Fisher-renormalization, the equation of state, and critical exponents, while the single-strand polymer relies on the double-strand polymer, vanishing at the critical point, yet possessing its own distinct critical exponents.

In the field of biomedicine, a crucial task is the creation of novel and diverse therapeutic antibody sequences that exhibit improved properties without compromising structural integrity. Recently, advancements in machine learning have been instrumental in tackling this challenge, specifically with deep language models and graph neural networks capable of antibody sequence generation. However, a major hurdle lies in training these models with limited available data, resulting in suboptimal performance and decreased sequence diversity. To address this issue, a new method, termed Model Reprogramming, repurposes pre-trained machine learning models to tackle the problem of sequence infilling in scarce data scenarios. Specifically, a new framework dubbed Reprogramming for Protein Sequence Infilling uses natural language models to generate novel protein sequences. This approach involves reformulating the problem of antibody sequence design as a text infilling task, where constant regions serve as sequence templates. Results demonstrate that reprogrammed models trained on a low-resourced antibody sequence dataset produce CDR sequences that exhibit a remarkable increase in diversity while maintaining naturalness. Furthermore, when compared to existing graph-based models that necessitate additional structural information, reprogrammed models prove particularly effective in designing longer CDR sequences and generating multiple loop regions simultaneously, all while displaying enhanced antigen binding capabilities.

Creating extensive, informative datasets is crucial for scientific advancement and development across diverse disciplines. Compiling large datasets, however, is a challenging task that demands the attention of both data creators and stakeholders. In our research, we outline the obstacles and advantages encountered during the development of a multinational European agricultural dataset with accurately labeled cultivated crops. This serves as a useful guide for anyone constructing their own dataset.

A key advantage of the Gaussian Process-based surrogate model within digital twin frameworks, specifically for accident tolerant fuel concepts, lies in its inherent ability to address issues arising from insufficient, incomplete, and inconsistent data. However, GP performance may be compromised when high-fidelity data is limited. Furthermore, GP-based approximation becomes increasingly challenging with higher dimensional functions, making noisy or erroneous data significant hurdles for advanced fuel concepts. Moreover, longer-term accident tolerant fuel candidates involve empirical differential equations, compounded by data availability issues. Notably, physics-informed multi-fidelity Kriging (MFK) offers significant potential for predicting required material properties, even when high-fidelity data is limited, making it particularly useful in the context of accident tolerant fuel research. In this chapter, MFK's applicability and benefits are demonstrated using experimental thermal conductivity data from accident tolerant fuel candidates, with MFK showing particular value when a small number of data points cannot be effectively modeled using conventional Kriging methods. Ultimately, MFK's integrated capability supports future stages of analysis and research in the development of digital twin systems for accident tolerant fuel.

A generalized method of reduction, based on Dirac realizations that expand on Poisson momentum maps, is established. The procedure yields several recognizable quasi-Poisson and Poisson geometric frameworks. Furthermore, we utilize this approach to introduce a novel reduction technique for a specified class of subgroup actions within quasi-Poisson geometry, leading to quasi-Poisson structures on specific spaces studied in geometric representation theory.

Single atoms have become crucial objects for researching quantum optics and processing quantum information.  The recent achievement of trapping and controlling individual atoms with precise optical dipole traps has sparked a surge of interest in this field.  Our study examines the behavior of atoms within an innovative dipole trap with a reversed beam direction, revealing a notable increase in the rate of atomic collisions.  The accompanying theoretical model anticipates significant rates of loading multiple atoms into the trap under optimal conditions.  This work introduces a novel strategy for regulating the behavior of a small number of atoms in a dipole trap, while also offering new avenues for the exploration of the collective effects that a small number of atoms have on quantum optics.

This research investigates the quantization of Carlip's novel model, which introduces a new method to relate boundary degrees of freedom to a black hole's stretched horizon, particularly for stationary non-extremal black holes. The developed path integral approach involves integrating over time-reparameterized degrees of freedom on the stretched horizon, maintaining a constant length. The associated symplectic form provides the necessary measure for the path integral. However, one-loop calculations reveal a divergence issue, potentially signifying instability in the classical solution or a deeper issue with the model. Furthermore, analytical continuation of the field results in a boundary partition function that's independent of inverse temperature, thereby making it irrelevant to thermodynamics at least at the one-loop level. This finding stands in contrast to similar research in JT gravity, which assigns the entirety of thermodynamic contributions to boundary degrees of freedom.

To boost performance in low-resource languages that struggle due to a lack of training data, we've developed an innovative multilingual training method called knowledge distillation. This method utilizes individual monolingual teacher models, which have been optimized for their native language and a balanced, reduced dataset, to distill their knowledge into a unified, multilingual student model. Compared to conventional training techniques, our approach not only excels in low-resource languages but also achieves improved performance in high-resource languages while requiring the same amount of training data. If implemented extensively, our approach has the potential to increase the presence of low-resource languages in NLP systems.

Microresonators have significantly impacted modern nonlinear and quantum optics through advancements in frequency conversion. This study proposes a theory for multimode second harmonic generation in microresonators under conditions where parametric conversion predominantly occurs within the pump spectrum due to an expansive range in resonator parameters. The experimentally observed spectral adjustability of sideband generation is characterized by a discrete series of Eckhaus instabilities. Furthermore, we observe transitions into modelocking and soliton generation, which exhibit double-pulse patterns in the pump field and exist outside the interval of bistability, often on a slightly curved foundation.

To study the conductance of SLG and BLG junctions, we first considered SLG with an applied band gap and then connected it to pristine BLG. We found that for large Fermi energy and a given bilayer region length, the conductance exhibits anti-resonances at regular intervals. We then examined the effect of band gap and bilayer configuration, observing minima in the conductance with AA-BLG stacking that remain constant for all bilayer lengths, but are sensitive to d in the case of AB-BLG, resulting in a global energy gap. In the second part, we considered pristine SLG connected to gapped-biased BLG, observing peaks in the conductance profile with distinct periods and shapes. We also noted the presence of Klein tunneling and anti-Klein tunneling, the former resulting in zero conductance, but only in the second configuration, and exhibiting anti-Klein tunneling when the bilayer length is less than 10, and conductance vanishes. We then investigated how conductance changes as the bias voltage is applied, observing diminishing anti-resonances for large bias voltage values in the case of AA-BLG, but different behavior in the case of AB-BLG, which starts to conduct at low E values and exhibits maxima and minima at different bias voltage levels.

SOLNP+ is a modern constrained nonlinear optimization solver, based on SOLNP, a derivative-free method initially proposed in 1989. To enhance performance, we integrated implicit filtering, a restart strategy, and a modern quadratic programming solver with the original algorithm. Implemented in ANSI C, SOLNP+ demonstrates improved speed and reliability under noisy conditions over its predecessor in MATLAB. The software, which can be accessed without cost, is hosted on GitHub at https://github.com/COPT-Public/SOLNP_plus.

A novel portfolio optimization approach that dynamically responds to a continuous flow of market data is introduced. The strategy ensures superior wealth growth, comparable to that of the optimal static rebalancing strategy, in relation to a specific mapping of market signals to predefined market conditions. When this mapping is drawn from a specific, finite-dimensional family of transformations, the new method asymptotically achieves near-optimal results.

A rapidly advancing medical imaging technique, photoacoustic tomography (PAT), uses non-ionizing laser pulses to generate sound waves within the subject, which are detected externally and translated into detailed body images through complex inversion processes. In the context of PAT, one key mathematical challenge lies in reconstructing the original function that produced the observed acoustic waves, which are solutions to a wave equation outside the subject. In our study, we investigate a specific version of this problem that employs the fractional wave equation and considers detectors positioned on the surface of a sphere and a plane. Our work aims to develop a method for reconstructing the original function based on measurements from the solutions to the fractional wave equation obtained from these spherical and planar detectors.

Small solar system bodies such as Trans-Neptunian objects and Centaurs occupying the outer regions exhibit distinct photometric traits affected by their changing angles relative to our vantage point.  By utilizing precise photometric measurements alongside light curves at various orbital locations, we can effectively recreate their photometric profiles and determine physical attributes including orientation, dimensions, mass density, and even unusual characteristics, such as irregularities from their typical spherical shapes or presence of rings.  The process and technique behind this analysis will be discussed, accompanied by a survey of specific Trans-Neptunian objects and Centaurs that have undergone photometric modeling.

A promising technology, Visible Light Communication, provides secure and efficient short-range optical connections between vehicles and infrastructure. Its use in automated driving applications is explored for increasing the reliability of autonomous vehicles. A novel VLC-based system is proposed to enhance the communication reliability between vehicles and infrastructure in automated valet parking systems, utilizing VLC's jam-free and location-specific properties. A novel indoor parking system is developed, which utilizes bidirectional VLC to facilitate vehicle and infrastructure data exchange through real-time map updates. This system enables seamless vehicle and infrastructure data transmission, achieving error-free data exchange between devices within a range of 33 meters, thereby facilitating the sharing of vehicle sensor data and camera feed in indoor parking environments.

Over the past decade, advancements in 3D graphics have enabled highly realistic renderings but this detail comes at a cost of size and complexity, necessitating simplification through compression, which degrades their appearance. To optimize user experience, visual quality must be assessed to find an optimal balance between visual quality and file size. Our study aims to develop methods for both subjective and objective quality evaluations of 3D graphics, starting with the creation of a large dataset featuring over 343k corrupted textures and models. We filtered the data to a challenging subset and collected 148,929 user ratings to train a quality assessment metric that outperformed existing methods in both our and additional experiments. We demonstrated the potential of our metric and dataset to investigate how distortions in different elements and model characteristics impact users' perceptions of 3D graphics quality.

A theoretical framework incorporating fractional calculus has been developed for assessing the nonlocal static behavior of curved cylindrical panels. This approach leverages the unique differ-integral properties of fractional derivatives to accurately model long-range interactions within curved structures. Fractional-order kinematic relations are utilized to create a consistent, physically grounded framework that accounts for nonlocal elastic interactions. To examine the behavior of these structures under realistic conditions, a fractional Finite Element Method is formulated, integrating first-order shear-deformable shell elements. This study involves computational analyses exploring the nonlocal behavior of curved structures using fractional order models.

Although seemingly dissimilar, various non-traditional and traditional Lagrangians generating identical equations of motion are discernible in form due to their respective absence or presence of recognizable energy-based components. Specifically, a distinct subgroup of these Lagrangians, characterized as null Lagrangians and their associated gauge functions, holds a unique ability to facilitate novel roles in dynamics. This particular subgroup comprises null Lagrangians, which are recognized for their capacity to induce non-dissipative forces. Conversely, non-standard null Lagrangians and their respective gauge functions have the capacity to introduce dissipation forces into dynamic systems, thereby offering a more comprehensive perspective of the roles null Lagrangians play in dynamics. The findings have also been demonstrated in Newton's laws with a discussion of Galilean invariance considered.

A comprehensive compilation of machine learning articles is presented, categorizing them based on the size of the training data - small (1-100), medium (101-10000), and large (10000+). The review provides a detailed overview of the intersection of synthesis, characterization, and prediction in the field. Bayesian optimization is the most prevalent in the smaller dataset group, whereas support vector machine techniques are dominant in the medium-sized dataset group. To enhance predictive capabilities and model transparency, researchers often combine machine learning methods with techniques such as feature selection, adaptive design, and domain expertise, alongside high-throughput experimentation. Cross-validation strategies help mitigate overoptimistic predictive results. Limited design spaces and data-intensive conditions facilitate new material discovery in smaller datasets. However, large datasets reveal that optimization's 'easy gains' have often been achieved, and models tend to perform poorly when extrapolating to untested materials. A surge in machine learning-based materials science studies, incorporating experimental or computational validation, reflects a blurring of the lines between materials informatics and materials science, ultimately accelerating real-world materials discoveries.

To overcome challenges in the development of retinal prostheses that can assist the blind, researchers create retinal models to accurately simulate the responses of Retinal Ganglion Cells. The main goal of these prosthetic devices is to empower visually impaired individuals with the ability to tackle complex, everyday tasks using their vision. In this paper, we present the concept of functional assessment (FA) of retinal models and a machine learning method used for this purpose. The approach feeds traditional classifiers with retinal responses generated from the models and assesses performance on tasks like object recognition and digit identification using standard benchmark datasets (CIFAR-10, MNIST, Fashion MNIST, and Imagenette). We examined various factors that affect the effectiveness of FA, including task dependency and input formatting, and discovered that the number of output neurons influences model accuracy. However, we also found that simply dividing input images does not yield noticeable improvement in accuracy. Moreover, we noticed that the quality of the dataset influences the model's performance (with MNIST and Fashion MNIST achieving above 80% accuracy, and CIFAR-10 and Imagenette approximately 40%). Furthermore, we discovered that the quality of a retinal model in predicting the responses of Retinal Ganglion Cells correlates positively with its performance in the FA test, but the latter can provide valuable insights into the quality of the resulting visual perception.

Reinforcement learning methods using transfer learning attempt to aid agents in adapting to new domains by utilizing knowledge learned from agents that have been trained in similar source domains. Although research has focused on knowledge transfer for tasks with varying reward functions and dynamics, less emphasis has been placed on knowledge transfer for tasks with different action sets. This study addresses knowledge transfer in tasks differing in action sets, presenting a method for shaping rewards using a similarity measure for source embeddings that can be applied to domains with both continuous and discrete action sets. Our approach's effectiveness is assessed in Acrobot-v1 and Pendulum-v0 environments with restricted action sets, and a comparison with two benchmarks shows mixed results: our method doesn't outperform baselines in continuous action sets but shows improvements in discrete action sets. Ultimately, we outline potential future developments for this research area.

Real-world networks often feature defined community structures, characterized by high connectivity between nodes within the same group.  To analyze and learn from these complex networks, we introduce MarkovGNN, a model capable of directly capturing community formation and evolution within distinct convolutional layers. Unlike typical Graph Neural Networks that treat the graph as static, MarkovGNN employs a Markov process to generate diverse community-aware stochastic matrices, utilizing these to create different layers. MarkovGNN is a versatile method adaptable to the majority of existing GNNs. Experimental results demonstrate MarkovGNN's superiority over other GNNs for tasks such as community clustering, node categorization, and visualization. The source code for MarkovGNN is openly available on GitHub.

Creating user-friendly interfaces for controlling robots with various, complex, and imperfect input methods (for instance, monitoring a person's eye movements through a webcam) is a complex issue, mainly because the system lacks a clear 'default' interface when it comes to inferring the user's intended action. Reinforcement learning that relies on online user feedback to gauge the system's performance provides an optimal solution, allowing the interface to adapt to each individual user's needs. Nevertheless, this method often necessitates an abundance of human-supervised data, particularly if feedback is sparse. A more efficient hierarchical solution is proposed, in which we first train a latent space of useful robot behaviors using offline data, and subsequently use this pre-trained space to focus on learning a mapping from user inputs to specific robot behaviors during online feedback. A crucial insight behind this method is that having access to a pre-trained policy allows the system to obtain more insights from sparse rewards than would be the case with standard reinforcement learning. By utilising the pre-trained policy, the system can, in retrospect, relabel the intended action during failed task executions, based on information gained from successful executions. We tested our method in a study with 12 participants, where participants performed various robotic manipulation tasks (operating a switch, retrieving objects from a cabinet, and turning a valve) using a webcam and their eye movements, and found that our method could efficiently learn the link between the 128-dimensional eye movement features and the 7-dimensional robotic torques from sparse feedback in less than 10 minutes, and was able to adapt seamlessly to changing user strategies and differing input methods.

Red-giant stars in binary systems are crucial subjects for examining the internal and external development of aging stars. Although 83 binary red giants have been identified, only about 40 have had their seismic properties and orbits well-defined, making this group relatively small in comparison to known oscillating stars. These systems are typically discovered via their signature in space-based photometry. However, due to limited data resolution, shorter orbital periods tend to be favored, making it predominantly easier to detect smaller orbits. Therefore, this particular collection leans heavily towards H-shell burning stars and contains limited examples of He-core burning stars in their final evolutionary stages. By utilizing data from the Kepler, K2, and TESS missions as well as the BRITE constellation mission, we were able to locate 99 systems that weren't known to contain an oscillating red giant. Expanding our approach enabled the discovery of a greater diversity of orbital periods in these systems, with the maximum being as high as 26000days, allowing a rich population of He-core burning stars that are crucial to a more complete comprehension of the aging process. Expanding this particular collection nearly threefold enhances its potential in supporting both seismological studies and research on tides when combined with the forthcoming Gaia data, allowing further examination of the internal and external development of aging stars through the examination of the systems in their totality.

In group testing for networks where the nodes interact and are correlated, like detecting the spread of disease, leveraging the relationships among nodes allows for significant reduction in the required tests. By using a graph G that describes the node interactions and modeling the nodes as having a shared state if connected in a faulty random graph formed by dropping edges with probability 1-r, we analyze the performance of group testing for various graph types. Lower and upper bounds are determined on the test requirements in terms of n, r, and the error target. Notably, the benefits of leveraging correlation can be seen in the ratio between the total number of nodes and the equivalent independent nodes, leading to substantial improvements. By illustrating how the expected component size affects the test requirements and developing a new approximation for d-regular trees, we establish strong dependence and new insight into component size distributions. Upper bounds are found by creating dense subgraphs that allow more nodes to share states. Notably, improvements factor log(1/r) are observed in cyclic and tree graphs. By contrast, when graph G has nearly twice the edges, the grid model experiences a drastic improvement of {(1-r) log(1/r)}, while the larger the edges in graphs such as stochastic block models (SBM), the greater the scalability in test requirements improvements.

Our study presents an experimental analysis of Doppler-free saturated absorption spectroscopy for BaF molecules cooled with buffer gas in a cryogenic cell maintained at 4 Kelvin. By achieving a resolution of nearly 19 MHz, our spectra far exceed previous absorption spectroscopy capabilities and accurately distinguish hyperfine transitions. Using these high-resolution spectra, we were able to model the excited A(v=0) state hyperfine splittings, discovering the previously underestimated value of approximately 18 MHz for the $A^2\Pi_{1/2}(v=0, J=1/2, +)$ state critical to BaF laser cooling processes. This new information fills a crucial gap in the understanding of BaF laser cooling techniques.

Inverse problems are prevalent across a range of fields from aerospace to medical research. These problems involve deducing the underlying cause from available observations, often complicated by non-linear, stochastic forward models. A potential solution lies in using neural networks which can be trained from noisy data and execute quickly once trained. Nonetheless, trained inverse models often lack inherent assurance of correctness, making them unsuitable for critical safety and accuracy applications. This work introduces a novel approach to validating the accuracy of neural networks used to address inverse problems by employing a piecewise linear approximation and formulating both models as mixed-integer programming. We validate this method with a practical airplane fuel level monitoring system, allowing neural networks to be confidently used in contexts from aerospace to medicine.

A crucial element of a mature software development process is thorough code review, 
which necessitates the identification of the most suitable reviewer. However, selecting 
an inadequate reviewer can hinder the development process and lead to more bugs. Current 
reviewer recommendation systems predominantly rely on past interactions, considering 
individuals who modified or reviewed a file previously as ideal candidates. We argue 
that while such approaches successfully identify skilled reviewers, they often overlook 
other qualified developers who, despite having relevant expertise, may have never engaged 
with specific modified files. To address this, we propose a novel method, CORAL, 
which constructs a socio-technical graph to identify knowledgeable reviewers for code 
review tasks, especially in large, complex projects where traditional methods falter.

We examine strategic interactions in sequential bargaining between a proposer and a veto player, whose preferences align with single-peaked models. The key issue lies in the proposer's uncertainty regarding the veto player's ideal position. Due to lack of commitment, when players prioritize long-term benefits, various dynamics emerge, including Coasian patterns where the veto player's information significantly weakens the proposer's bargaining advantage. Contrary to expectations, our primary findings reveal the presence of equilibria that enable the proposer to achieve an optimal outcome, comparable to one obtained through binding commitments. The primary driving force behind this is the proposer's capacity to capitalize on the veto player's single-peaked preferences by creating an early opportunity to secure agreement from lower surplus groups and subsequently credibly negotiate a greater share of the surplus with higher surplus groups later on. To derive these insights, we take advantage of the theoretical link between sequential bargaining processes and static mechanisms used in game design.

Optimizing D2D communications relies heavily on effectively scheduling links to prevent excessive interference.  Existing approaches focus primarily on system throughput or fairness, overlooking information freshness.  A novel D2D link scheduling scheme is proposed in this study to jointly optimize age of information and throughput.  The motivation stems from the observation that maximum throughput scheduling can lead to poor information age performance by underutilizing links with suboptimal channel conditions.  A comprehensive model of spatiotemporal interfering queues under the LCFS-PR policy has been developed, enabling the derivation of expressions for average AoI and network throughput.  A neural network architecture has been designed to map geographic locations to optimal scheduling parameters, enabling decision-making without CSI after network training.  A method for backpropagating implicit loss functions through a numerical solution to gradients has been developed, enabling the validation of performance through comparison with local optimal algorithms exhibiting high computational complexity.  Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed approach yields comparable performance to optimal local algorithms while offering reduced complexity, highlighting a trade-off between age of information and network throughput.

Recent findings demonstrate that under specified conditions for a kernel K on domain Omega in C to the power of m, the derived expression from the interaction between the kernel squared and the curvature of logarithmically transformed kernel also fulfills non-negative definiteness. Building upon this result, two key consequences are examined within this paper, including an extension of a curvature inequality for specific operator classes and a correlation between the reproducing kernels of certain modules with the curvature of their respective quotient modules.

Researchers working with the Event Horizon Telescope have created detailed images of black holes in the Milky Way and a nearby galaxy called M87. Future advancements in technology will allow them to generate detailed maps showing the spectral characteristics of black hole activity. To predict such maps for two significant black holes, Sgr A* and M87*, the research team applied complex models to simulations. Their calculations revealed that certain properties of black hole activity contribute to variations in the spectral characteristics, resulting in more negative readings closer to the black hole. These findings suggest that analyzing spectral characteristics could aid in distinguishing between competing models of black hole behavior. However, accurately determining this spectral data heavily depends on the current understanding of plasma physics. Despite the uncertainty, future improvements could enable the differentiation of various black hole models by analyzing spectral characteristics even in cases where the activity is not fully resolved, like the activity around Sgr A* at 230 GHz. Specifically, two distinct black hole models - the Standard and Normal Evolution model and the Magnetically Arrested Disk model - can be distinguished by comparing the spectral characteristics due to inherent differences in the temperature and magnetic properties of the black hole activity.

Precise forecasts of uncertainty in treatment doses during radiation therapy are critical to creating reliable treatment plans, requiring solutions to particle transport problems with uncertain parameters or starting conditions. In these situations, where high accuracy is paramount, Monte Carlo methods often prevail. Nonetheless, conventional non-intrusive strategies, involving repeated simulations at different parameter values, can be unfeasible due to their lengthy computational times. Conversely, intrusive methods may limit integration with commercial simulation software. We had earlier explored the use of an innovative uncertainty quantification approach in our research involving proton dose calculations with normal error distributions on authentic patient data. In this study, we present a more comprehensive theoretical examination of the approach in regards to bias, errors, and convergence of the predictions. Additionally, our multivariate model of input variables allows for flexible and accurate correlation of errors. We showcase how this framework enables the efficient analysis and quantification of complex interrelated and time-sensitive uncertainties.

Mode-locked fiber lasers offer a significant challenge in generating soliton molecules (SMs) with a precise time interval. To overcome this issue, we devised a laser system utilizing second-order group-velocity dispersion and controlled loss rates to engineer SM dynamics. This approach allowed us to balance dispersion and nonlinearity using the real part of dispersion and optimize gain through the dispersion loss rate. Consequently, we were able to select desired temporal separations in bound SM pairs and achieve tunability of central wavelengths. Furthermore, our setup enabled the creation of multiple SMs with predetermined time separations and central wavelengths, demonstrating its potential in the design of advanced optical data-processing systems.

The analysis of oscillators that lose energy due to coupling is complex and significant in power grids, requiring new methods that traditional techniques can't provide due to a lack of symmetry caused by this energy loss. This study reveals a connection between stable synchronization in these oscillators and their state space, particularly with the concept of a winding partition, a geometric idea influenced by network topology. Utilizing the winding partition, the accompanying algorithms enable computation of all synchronous solutions in networks of dissipatively coupled oscillators, providing valuable insights into anomalous behaviors in lossy network systems. Notably, the study challenges conventional expectations by showing that loop flows and energy dissipation can increase a system's ability to transfer energy and that energy dissipation can foster coexistence of multiple stable states. Furthermore, the developed geometric framework is applied to a well-established power grid test case, revealing two high-voltage solutions characterized by distinct loop flows.

Atomistic simulations require a fundamental input called interatomic potentials (IAPs), which depict the potential energy of atoms. Currently available IAPs are either restricted to limited chemical systems or lack accuracy in general use. This study introduces a universal IAP called M3GNet that utilizes graph neural networks with three-body interactions to model atom behavior. M3GNet's vast database encompasses ten years of structural relaxations provided by the Materials Project, enabling applications across structural relaxation, dynamic simulations, and property predictions for various materials. From over 31 million crystal structures, approximately 1.8 million potentially stable materials were discovered, and through further analysis, DFT calculations confirmed 1578 of the top 2000 materials with low energies above hull as being truly stable. This machine learning approach has the potential to accelerate the discovery of materials possessing remarkable properties that can be synthesized.

In 2019, Qiao, Duan, and Cheng presented a novel method for distributed nearest-neighbor classification, where large datasets are fragmented into smaller segments that each employ a k-nearest-neighbor classifier. These classifiers then combine their results using a majority vote to determine the final class label. Their research reveals that by dividing the data into a large number of groups and setting k to 1, this distributed algorithm achieves a nearly optimal error rate, relative to standard algorithms, for both regression and classification tasks. Furthermore, for classification with a specified number of groups M, this distributed approach is shown to perform comparably to standard algorithms. To optimize this process, additional classification methods were developed, and their effectiveness in attaining the optimal rates was demonstrated.

In next-generation networks, including 5G/6G, maintaining a high Quality of Experience (QoE) is vital for multimedia service delivery, and this requires accurate quality monitoring, prediction, and resource allocation capabilities where machine learning can significantly contribute. This paper provides a tutorial on designing and implementing QoE measurement and forecasting systems for video streaming services using supervised learning-based models. First, a comprehensive pipeline for developing and deploying QoE prediction models is outlined, encompassing data acquisition, feature engineering, model fine-tuning, and assessment. Second, a framework for deploying QoE prediction systems in future networks is proposed using networking technologies like Software-Defined Networking, Network Function Virtualization, and Mobile Edge Computing. Lastly, a comparison is conducted among current state-of-the-art machine learning models for predicting video streaming QoE performance metrics.

The introduction of Generative Adversarial Imitation Learning (GAIL) has led to a surge of interest in adversarial imitation learning (AIL) methods, particularly with the development of ValueDice, which outperforms classical Behavioral Cloning (BC) and GAIL under certain settings. We investigate whether ValueDice's advantages stem from advanced algorithm designs. Our analysis yields the following findings: first, ValueDice can be reduced to BC in offline settings; second, overfitting is present and regularization is essential in low-data regimes; third, BC with weight decay can approach expert performance as ValueDice; and finally, ValueDice's success hinges on complete expert trajectories rather than subsampling. Our results shed light on imitation learning beyond ValueDice.

To study exchange bias effects, ultrathin bilayers of permalloy and cobalt oxide were deposited on a nanomechanical resonator with a novel design. The removal of one arm significantly improved the mechanical response of the resonator to torques in three different directions. Our innovative method allows us to measure three orthogonal torque components simultaneously. Through experiments at extremely low temperatures, the anisotropies caused by exchange coupling at interfaces were measured, confirming the presence of exchange bias between the permalloy and cobalt oxide layers. Furthermore, an in-plane rotating bias field was used to examine the in-plane anisotropies through the out-of-plane torque, demonstrating that the characteristics associated with interfacial coupling remained even after considerable training. The observed data from rotational hysteresis loops were analyzed and fit using a solution based on the Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert equation, where each parameter of the exchange bias model accounts for distinct features in the loops.

In traditional graph-based recommendation systems, the information for users and items is pre-compiled, which isn't suitable for real-world applications with continuously flowing data streams. Updating predictions for the changing model would necessitate repeatedly retraining models, a practically infeasible solution.  In this study, a compositional recommendation model known as Lightweight Compositional Embedding (LCE) was proposed, capable of supporting efficient incremental updates under low computational costs. Rather than learning embeddings for the complete set of nodes, LCE uses explicit embeddings for a subset and implicitly represents others via composition functions based on their graph interactions. Our analysis of user-item interaction data on a large scale, under streaming conditions, highlights LCE's superior performance over competing models, with nearly optimal results and significantly fewer parameters required.

Continuous integration of new data using Bayes' theorem can be achieved through online learning by an agent; yet, applying Bayesian methods in non-static environments results in a slow adaptation to changes in the environment. The outcome can be state estimates confidently converging on a wrong parameter value. To handle the issue of adapting to changes in non-static environments, it's common practice to either discard or down-weight old data; however, forgetting in this context fails to address that many environments require the re-visit to similar situations or scenarios. To handle the issue of adapting to changes in non-static environments while utilizing previous experience, we suggest an advanced system called Bayes with Adaptive Memory (BAM). This new framework allows the system to decide what data points it remembers and what data points it discards. Our results demonstrate that our framework generalizes several Bayesian update rules designed for changing environments, including the various types of experiments, demonstrating its ability to constantly adjust as per the continuously changing environment.

Research into out-of-distribution generalization by neural networks has gained prominence, driven by increasing evidence of their vulnerability to distribution shifts.  Most studies to date have focused on Euclidean data and the challenges associated with adapting to graph-structured data have yet to be fully addressed.  The complexities of graph data include not only inter-connectional variability but also inherent structural information.  In an effort to tackle this issue, a new invariant learning approach is presented in this study, specifically a method called Explore-to-Extrapolate Risk Minimization (EERM). EERM uses multiple graph editors that are trained to increase the variance of risks in multiple virtual environments, thereby facilitating the model to make predictions beyond its training environment.  The theoretical soundness of this method has been validated and it is demonstrated that EERM is effective in addressing real-world data problems involving artificial spurious features, cross-domain transfers, and dynamic graph evolution.

In recent times, techniques representing data as graphs such as Graph Neural Networks have shown effectiveness in learning data representations to solve a wide range of problems, including classification and link prediction. The applications of these methods are extensive, but existing work primarily relies on a fixed graph structure. This limitation is significant in rapidly changing systems with non-static connections and unknown structures, resulting in sub-optimal performance. By contrast, adapting models to account for changing connections in real-time can uncover valuable insights, going beyond standard classification tasks. The majority of current methods fail to effectively learn connections and rely on cross-node correlations to generate graphs without direction. This limitation is a significant shortcoming, particularly in fields such as neuroscience, where direction is crucial. Our proposed DECENNT model bridges this gap by training neural networks to derive interpretable dynamic and directed graphs specific to classification or prediction tasks. DECENNT significantly outperforms current methods across five different tasks and produces dynamic, interpretable graphs, including functional graphs aligning with established knowledge in the field and providing new insights. The temporal attention module within DECENNT can pinpoint the specific intervals of multivariate time series that are crucial for accurate prediction.

Using Principal Component Analysis, researchers investigate the hydrodynamic attractor in Yang-Mills kinetic theory under Color Glass Condensate initial conditions and Bjorken expansion. This attractor at late times is determined by a principal component that controls the total energy level, which is achieved through the elimination of lower-order principal components representing deviations in pressure anisotropy, mass screening, and scattering rates. We find that the hydrodynamic attractor approach at late times is typically modeled using an exponential function, with its decay rate linked to the coupling, ultimately reducing to a relationship with the shear viscosity to entropy density ratio.

We developed a cellular automaton decoder that significantly enhances active quantum error-correction methods by utilizing robust properties in self-correcting quantum memories. This decoder was specifically designed for the XYZ color code, which involves locally rotating the bases of physical qubits. When noise predominantly causes dephasing, the decoder exhibits properties of a two-dimensional fractal code without the presence of string-like logical operators. In high-noise environments, the local decoder mimics the performance of a partially self-correcting memory. Our simulations also revealed that at low error rates, the memory duration increases exponentially with system size without the aid of a global decoder, up to a certain system size limit that grows as the error rate is lowered. Moreover, despite not replicating partially self-correcting behavior in moderate-noise scenarios, our numerical results show longer memory times at noise biases that reflect real-world conditions. Our findings suggest the potential design of customized cellular automaton decoders to alleviate the bandwidth demands of global decoding under realistic noise models.

The use of random quantum circuits extends to a broad range of areas, from quantum computers to studying black holes. A crucial factor is their ability to mimic randomness: These circuits approximate unitary t-designs, which mimic Haar randomness up to a certain threshold. A landmark study found that for a brickwork qubit architecture, depth is key to this mimicry. A recent examination has updated this finding, determining a lower limit on the spectral gap of certain circuit components is related to circuit depth, which has now been refined to be more efficient than initially found. A byproduct of this refinement is the ability of circuits to mimic Haar randomness more effectively in less steps, which has significant implications for the broader field of quantum studies. To reach this conclusion, specific quantum and statistical concepts have been applied and tested in different scenarios, such as quantum unitary distributions that involve different types of operations.

Smart home presence detection is an advancing field of study that requires determining whether a household is occupied, which has significant implications in various contexts. These contexts include the care for the elderly, individuals with dementia, and those undergoing home quarantine. While previous research relied heavily on sensors that track door movements and camera monitoring to detect a resident's outing, these approaches have significant drawbacks. They are intrusive and necessitate modifications for optimal placement. Our research takes a different approach by examining how appliance electrical usage can indicate a resident's presence or absence, utilizing a non-invasive sensing method that dissects power consumption patterns. Due to a lack of publicly available datasets for this specific application, artificial scenarios were created on a renowned dataset for Non-Intrusive Load Monitoring, and subsequent machine learning assessments demonstrated that absence detection via appliance power analysis is indeed viable.

Our proposed approach represents the first comprehensive learning-based method for near-field Photometric Stereo imaging, in which nearby light sources are utilized for 3D object reconstruction.  Given its efficiency, it can be especially useful for modeling static objects of large scale, and can produce results within a second, which can be beneficial for AR and VR applications. Prior methods for near-field Photometric Stereo predominantly employed optimization along with a far-field neural network operating at the pixel or patch level. However, due to optimization, existing techniques often encounter performance issues (requiring a significant amount of  GPU memory and being computationally slow), whereas focusing on pixels or patches results in susceptibility to noise and calibration inaccuracies. In contrast, our recursive multi-resolution framework estimates surface normals and depth maps for entire images by iteratively computing depth and 'per-pixel' illumination values. Compared to current techniques, which are often hampered by iterative optimization, our approach yields an approximately 45x improvement in processing time and enhanced precision (resulting in a Mean Angular Error of 11.3 degrees as opposed to 13.3 degrees) for near-field Photometric Stereo reconstruction.

In recent years, advancements have been seen in the applications of light field technology, particularly in light field rendering and depth estimation. Although cutting-edge light field rendering techniques efficiently handle objects with semi-transparent or reflective properties, depth estimation methods fall short, often either ignoring such cases entirely or only providing mediocre results. We believe this is because existing methods only account for a single, correct depth value when in reality multiple objects at different depths contribute to a pixel's color. To address this, we propose using a novel approach where a posterior depth distribution is output instead of a single estimate. We explore and develop several deep-learning-based solutions and introduce a pioneering'multimodal light field depth dataset', providing depths for each contributing object to facilitate multimodal depth prediction and method validation via KL divergence measurement.

We have assembled a comprehensive catalog containing 65,981 Mira-type variable stars from the OGLE project's database, with two-thirds of them located within the Milky Way's Galactic bulge regions. A significant majority of the stars, at 47,532, were newly identified in this study. We have collected observational data and light curve measurements of the stars across various wavelengths and provided access to a time-series photometry database spanning from 1997. Utilizing manual light curve inspections by experienced astronomers resulted in a high level of catalog accuracy. We also estimate a 96% completeness rate by leveraging overlapping fields in the dataset. A comparative analysis is presented, examining statistical patterns among Miras within different areas of the galaxy and highlighting instances where star types have transitioned over time. The dataset offers valuable insights for investigating the Milky Way's three-dimensional structure and may shed light on the enigma of the X-shaped bulge.

In this study, a novel, compact image segmentation model named L^3U-net is developed that operates efficiently in real-time on limited resource edge devices. To enhance processing speed, a data processing technique called data folding is utilized, which effectively leverages the capabilities of parallelized convolutional neural network accelerators. Upon implementing the model on a MAX78000 device, experimental outcomes reveal that L^3U-net yields superior results, attaining accuracy of more than 90% on multiple image segmentation datasets at a rate of approximately 10 frames per second.

We calculated a new measurement of the Hubble constant using the recession rate of Earth's Moon from data derived through sedimentary and eclipse-based lunar movement assessments. This value of 63.01 $\pm$ 1.79 km s$^{-1}$ Mpc$^{-1}$ closely aligns with Planck's findings based on cosmic microwave background observations and $\Lambda$CDM theory, while also serving as the first ever measurement that does not rely on models or multiple steps. This estimate, which represents a major breakthrough in measuring the local universe's expansion rate, is also notably lower than other recent $H_0$ determinations and resistant to certain sources of systematic error seen in other measurement methods such as supernovae or quasars. The work provides evidence that discrepancies between various Hubble constant measurements could indeed result from issues within the local distance ladder method.

Developing automatic speech recognition systems for multiple languages, especially Indic languages, poses difficulties due to acoustic and lexical differences. This problem is further complicated by the lack of open-source data sets for various methods. In this research, we compare the effectiveness of end-to-end multilingual ASR models with single-language models utilizing language identification technology. Utilizing language detection from a multilingual model, combined with individual monolingual models, yields significant improvement of 50% word error rate across languages. Moreover, our approach addresses Code Switched difficulties and attains impressive WER metrics of 21.77 and 28.27 for Hindi-English and Bengali-English combinations, respectively. This research highlights the potential of using transformer-based ASR models, specifically wav2vec 2.0, in multilingual ASR and Code Switched ASR applications for Indic languages.

The mystery of dark matter may be better understood with data from high-redshift space observations. The presence of interactions between dark matter and ordinary matter influences the development of cosmic dawn and the ionization process, resulting in colder gas temperatures. The effect of these interactions on temperature fluctuations in matter and dark matter, however, has not yet been fully explored. This study determines these effects, tracing the development of cosmic perturbations from the dark ages forward, and reveals significant consequences for cosmic dawn. The study demonstrates a substantial change in temperature fluctuations on large scales and an increased suppression in matter power at a specific wavelength, with an example computation of the HI power spectrum revealing significant discrepancies due to changes in temperature and ionization power. The study concludes that these interactions must be considered in models examining cosmic dawn and the ionization process, based on observable differences from current predictions.

Recent advancements in learning from minimal supervision have sparked efforts to design models capable of identifying unfamiliar categories during testing. These generalized zero-shot learning (GZSL) approaches rely on knowledge of all categories beforehand, either with or without labeled data. Nevertheless, practical scenarios demand adaptable models that can incorporate newly emerging classes dynamically (continual generalized zero-shot learning or CGZSL). Sequentially retraining and reusing conventional GZSL methods has shown to suffer from the drawback of catastrophic forgetting and suboptimal performance. Recent endeavors towards tackling CGZSL are often hampered by differences in methodologies, data partitions, and protocols employed, leading to challenging comparisons and unclear paths forward. In light of these considerations, this work firstly streamlines various CGZSL settings into a unified framework and introduces the 'Online-CGZSL' variant. We propose a unified framework that incorporates bidirectional incremental alignment to enable the dynamic adaptation of models in response to new, either seen or unseen classes that arrive over time across any of these CGZSL settings. Extensive experiments and analyses on five benchmark datasets have demonstrated that our method consistently outperforms current approaches, especially when implemented in the 'Online' setting.

As research into dark matter (DM) expands to include self-annihilation and thermal components, incorporating a wide range of relevant processes is crucial for improving prediction accuracy, particularly those directly tied to DM properties. We're studying how DM subhalos interact with Sommerfeld enhancement of annihilation cross-sections, including both s-wave and p-wave cases, as these factors are vital in thermal DM particle searches for masses exceeding the TeV range, or when there's a relatively light dark sector. We provide a comprehensive analytical analysis of these interactions, illustrating their scaling in relation to subhalo masses and Sommerfeld parameters. We derive approximate formulas that simplify understanding intricate phenomena and enhance gamma-ray signal predictions for diverse target masses, from dwarf galaxies to galaxy clusters, significantly raising expectations. The combination of subhalos and Sommerfeld effect amplifies the annihilation signal, particularly on resonances, making them crucial for producing reliable predictions.

We conducted a study combining $\it{Herschel}$-SPIRE imaging with data from CFIS, using UNIONS low surface brightness data to measure correlations between cosmic infrared and optical backgrounds. Utilizing $91\,{\rm deg}^2$ of data with a minimum resolved scale of $18\,$arcsec, we examined two scenarios where either all visible galaxies were included or individually-detected galaxies were masked, generating background maps. Notably, a correlation signal exceeding 22 standard deviations ($\gtrsim 18\,\sigma$ for the background maps) was discovered, with fluctuations attributed to an $r$ band optical brightness level of $\simeq 32.5\,{\rm mag}\,{\rm arcsec}^{-2}$, a magnitude unachievable through standard source-by-source examination. However, a primary challenge is determining the degree of contamination caused by emission from Galactic cirrus; although the contamination varies greatly, with one field exhibiting roughly a tenfold greater extragalactic signal than the other field. Nevertheless, a second discriminant was identified where the cross-power spectrum follows the pattern $P(k)\propto 1/k$ which deviates from Galactic cirrus patterns. Utilizing this novel approach in a halo-model framework showed a satisfactory correlation with prior studies and measurements of galaxy star-formation rates. Future projects combining FYST/CCAT-prime, Euclid, or LSST hold significant potential to explore star-formation galaxy evolution with higher detail and precision.

Filamentous cyanobacteria, consisting of elongated cells linked together, have thrived on Earth as one of the earliest forms of life and exhibit organized collective behavior. They form complex structures and patterns such as biomats and stromatolites due to their mechanical properties.  The properties of these cyanobacteria like rigidity play a key role in their biological success.  Specifically, their ability to resist deformation through the bending modulus, or flexural rigidity, makes them suitable for algae-based biofuel production among other applications.
