We argue that beyond four qubits, these patterns do not change, although their complexity grows as qubit numbers increase. We identify a point at four qubits beyond which some stabilizer states are inconsistent with holographic principles. We reflect on the characteristics of this phase transition as observed in the stabilizer reachability graphs.

The MultiEarth 2022 competition represents the inaugural event focused on
forest surveillance and deforestation analysis within the Amazon rainforest
regardless of weather and time. Its primary objective is to provide a unified
benchmark for processing multiple information types, thereby facilitating
cross-disciplinary collaboration among environmental and Earth science
experts alongside multimodal representation learning specialists. To evaluate
various learning techniques' effectiveness in predicting deforestation, MultiEarth
2022 will be divided into three components: 1) filling data gaps, 2) estimating
forest clearance rates, and 3) image transformation. This paper provides
detailed instructions for each component, alongside the relevant data sets and
evaluation metrics. Access the challenge information at https://sites.google.com/view/rainforest-challenge.

Recent studies have highlighted the significance of achieving equilibrium among conflicting goals in model development, including accuracy versus fairness, or disparate measures of fairness. This balance represents a broader spectrum of multi-objective optimization problems, where optimization techniques strive to discover Pareto optimal compromises between competing objectives. Our work initiates with the introduction of a differentiable metric allowing for direct optimization of group fairness in model development, particularly, achieving balance in accuracy across different groups. Subsequently, we introduce two model-agnostic multi-objective optimization frameworks to train neural classification models over varying groups of neural architectures, attaining Pareto optimal parameterizations. Our frameworks were put to the test on the specific task of hate speech identification, a domain in which earlier studies have documented a lack of fairness across speakers of diverse English dialects. Experimental outcomes across different architectures, including convolutional, sequential, and transformer-based models, reveal superior trade-offs between accuracy and fairness compared to existing research. Most notably, our measure empowers the Pareto optimization process to guarantee that each model attains the optimal trade-off between fairness and accuracy relative to the dataset, adhering to user-prescribed tolerance bounds.

Graphene's electronic properties can be modified through established intercalation methods. This technique not only produces stable, two-dimensional elements but also creates unique interfaces with quantum confinement. Our study features monolayer graphene on silicon carbide, where the addition of lead creates an electrically neutral state and unusually high p-type charge carrier density. By analyzing the electronic structure, we find new bands related to 2D lead at the interface. Our findings, confirmed through additional experiments, show 2D confinement and resulting superconductivity at the graphene-silicon carbide interface. These results open the possibility of exploring spin-orbit effects or 2D superconductivity.

Conversational AI systems typically evaluate response candidates based on the similarity between their representations and the context, using a single text form for the context, which limits its ability to generalize. This paper introduces a framework that incorporates multiple variations of a dialogue context to enhance learning, using a secondary learning goal based on contrastive learning to create more resilient representations. By augmenting dialogue context with perturbations through a contrastive learning method, we can achieve better results in conversational ranking, especially when paired with current augmentation methods and the BERT-based architecture. Our proposed augmentation method, ConMix, injects perturbations at the token level, using a random mix of tokens from various dialogue contexts within a batch. Our research showcases the benefits of our proposed augmentation method over previous approaches, demonstrating the potential to create more robust and generalizable dialogue representations.

Imitation learning can enable robots to acquire fine motor manipulation skills efficiently without extensive computational costs. Nevertheless, present imitation learning approaches necessitate sophisticated data collection systems and have difficulty generalizing beyond their original parameters. One way to overcome this constraint is by gathering additional data representing real-world operating conditions. This work focuses on characteristics of such additional training data, examining its effect on a robot's ability to complete complex tasks like grasping and placement. Our research reveals that corrective demonstrations greatly outperform randomly sampled demonstrations when there's a substantial difference in their proportion to the original demonstrations. In contrast, there's little distinction between these two methods when there's a considerable surplus of original demonstrations. Our results illustrate a trade-off between collecting corrective demonstrations and their enhanced performance. Furthermore, we've found that vision-based sensors, such as the LeapMotion, can substantially decrease the expense of acquiring demonstrations for complex manipulation tasks. Our related source code is publicly available.

This study details a BLCU-ICALL system that successfully participated in the Definition Modeling subtrack of the 2022 SemEval Task 1, specifically Comparing Dictionaries and Word Embeddings. The system excelled, achieving a 1st-place ranking for Italian, 2nd place for Spanish and Russian, and a 3rd-place finish for both English and French. To tackle this challenge, we developed a multitasking transformer-based framework that synergizes diverse embedding architectures through cross-attention and models gloss structures with a masked language model objective. We also explored the effectiveness of combining our models through ensembling for added robustness. The evaluation results confirm the effectiveness of our solution. The corresponding code can be accessed via the BLCU-ICALL GitHub repository: https://github.com/blcuicall/SemEval2022-Task1-DM.

Understanding the life cycles of stars and the structure of our galaxy depends on observing open clusters in a synchronized manner. Thanks to the accurate measurement of stars' distances and movement patterns, it is now possible to isolate these clusters from their surroundings more effectively. However, studies involving many clusters face challenges because current methods rely mainly on observations at visible light wavelengths. Our research takes a new approach by incorporating near-infrared data into open clusters sequences observed by the Gaia space mission and the VVV survey. By applying advanced statistical analysis on a dataset consisting of 37 open clusters, we achieved a reliable separation of cluster members from background stars using a specialized algorithm that involves two stages: an initial coarse analysis and a subsequent detailed investigation of 8 key characteristics. Our investigation found that, on average, nearly 50% more likely candidate cluster members could be identified at near-infrared wavelengths, compared to previous studies, when we only considered sources with a high probability of being part of the cluster. Our work is part of a broader effort aimed at producing accurate open clusters sequences using a unified approach.

This survey chronicles the developments over the past decade in efficiently tackling the complexity of solving constraint satisfaction problems within the frameworks of the streaming and sketching computational models. The survey outlines some of the key findings and offers insight into the underlying proof structures, specifically focusing on the existence of a dichotomous outcome where algorithms operating within a subpolynomial space exhibit a tight dichotomy.

The way Earth's and other planets' rotation responds to gravitational pulls is deeply influenced by their internal composition.  One notable phenomenon known as the Free Core Nutation mode significantly amplifies nutation effects in a specific frequency band.  However, this mode is also similar in nature and frequency to the Spin-Over Mode, where a planet's core oscillates due to rotation.  Through a detailed analysis of a planetary model featuring a non-fluid core and a freely rotating core with an inviscid fluid core, we found that the Spin-Over Mode corresponds to the point at which a planet's external and internal forces balance out and its mantle becomes steadily rotating.  Additionally, the presence of energy loss at the core-mantle boundary affects the resonance frequency of the Free Core Nutation.  We discovered that this resonance shift, estimated to be approximately one day for Earth, is likely the result of the proximity between the two frequency modes.  Moreover, this close alignment results in a slightly reduced Quality factor of the resonance compared to the value derived using conventional calculations.  Finally, we discuss the implications of this mechanism for the rotation patterns of Mars, the Moon, and the Earth's long-term rotation behavior.

The infrared hyperspectral imaging technique is gaining traction in the fields of materials and life sciences but faces limitations in sub-diffraction nanoimaging, where it processes data sequentially. A novel method combining atomic force microscopy with infrared spectroscopy (AFM-IR) has been proposed using low-rank matrix reconstruction to optimize the efficiency of hyperspectral infrared nanoimaging. A study utilized the Leishmania parasite as a biologically relevant target and applied a 220nm resolution in the mid-infrared range to collect high-resolution data. Following hierarchical cluster analysis, a small data set was used to test low-rank matrix recovery for the full data set. Evaluating results indicated notable agreements in the data reconstruction between the original and the low-rank recovery process, thus reducing the data collection time significantly from 14 hours to under one hour. The proposed technique is expected to increase the applicability of hyperspectral nanoimaging in the analysis of both nanomaterials and biological substances in research and industrial contexts.

Our research investigates the thermal emission of photons from the quark-gluon plasma at a specific temperature, and it utilizes spatial vector correlators computed using lattice QCD and perturbative QCD theories. We analyze these correlators at a fixed spatial momentum and observe that lattice QCD correlators align closely with both perturbative QCD and supersymmetric Yang-Mills theories. To refine our findings, we apply a specific data analysis technique to compare and filter the correlators. Based on these studies, we develop models that fit the data well for low-frequency photons, and use these models to determine the high-frequency behavior. We then compare our findings for photon emissivity to previous results and derive a precise constraint on the differential photon emission rate, specifically around 0.8 GeV, resulting in a rate of approximately 2.2 x 10^-3 GeV.

Following the discovery of magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene, research has centered around exploiting the potential of flat bands in Dirac materials to create robust correlation effects in electronic systems. We demonstrate that the underlying symmetry group of a Dirac material plays a pivotal role in determining whether the material's flatness can be engineered by adjusting a small number of variables. We develop a framework to compute, given a symmetry group, the exact number of variables needed to zero out the Dirac velocity, thereby making the material's flatness accessible. This method is then applied to examine the potential for flat band formation in twisted bilayer graphene and topological insulator surface states. Based on these insights, we determine the specific symmetries required for a Dirac velocity of zero to result in perfectly-flat bands, thereby broadening the understanding of what constitutes flat-band topological materials. Furthermore, we construct theoretical models exhibiting flat-band topological behavior in well-defined regions of parameter space: one is a theoretical analogue of two 3D TI surfaces, and the other is a quasi-crystalline modification of the TBG chiral model.

We investigate controlling systems that are described by complex and randomly influenced equations, where each component's behavior has an impact on the others. For such systems, we establish a method to determine their behavior relative to one another and introduce a new framework that transforms their behavior into a simpler, more predictable form. This new framework allows for a control strategy that makes the system behave predictably and consistently. However, we note that this strategy is idealized, as it relies on something that is not actually measurable, thus making it impossible to apply in reality. Building on the principles of this idealized strategy, we design a new approach that integrates different control mechanisms. This new approach achieves a level of control that is similar to the idealized one when it has the capability to constantly adjust for errors. We examine the possibility of accurately replicating a specific outcome and solve it for both the idealized and the practical framework. To demonstrate the practicality of our new approach, we apply it to a hypothetical situation.

C/2017 K2, a comet from the Oort Cloud, was initially seen in action when it was at least 20 AU from the Sun, marking what likely was its first entry into the inner solar system. On 2021 March 19-20, the comet was captured by the Hubble Space Telescope (HST) at 6.82 AU and an 8.35-degree phase angle, before it experienced significant water ice sublimation on its surface. Through observations, the properties of the dust surrounding the comet were analyzed, indicating radial variations in color and polarization. Specifically, the color gradient of the dust increased with distance from the comet nucleus. Furthermore, the dust intensity patterns did not match predictions of how stable dust particles would behave. Subsequent near-infrared images taken at the Palomar Hale Telescope in May revealed a distinct absence of micron-sized particles in the comet's tail but found no spatial variation in JHKs colors. These findings suggest the comet's inner coma consisted mostly of tiny, rapidly sublimating water ice grains rather than larger, stable dust grains found in the tail. A comparison of these findings to observations of another Oort Cloud comet, C/2012 S1, reveals the possibility of an observational error having occurred in earlier research regarding the near-nucleus polarimetric halo of this particular comet.

Quantum computing offers the potential to greatly accelerate computationally
intensive tasks such as solving complex problems involving numerous elements.
Research has explored the application of quantum-assisted algorithms in
particle physics, specifically in rapidly grouping particles into jets in
high-energy collisions. This study evaluates quantum annealing methods for jet
clustering, utilizing optimization of the 'thrust' parameter in electron-positron
collisions to gauge performance. The results indicate that quantum annealing
performs comparably to classical exact methods and traditional classical heuristics
only when optimized through parameter tuning. However, when parameters aren't fine-
tuned, similar outcomes can be achieved through the combination of quantum and
classical approaches.

We introduce cross-view transformers, a streamlined, attention-based model for
semantic map segmentation from multiple camera angles. Our model inherently maps
distinct camera perspectives onto a standard map layout using an innovative
cross-view attention mechanism that considers each camera's specific calibration.
Each camera employs positional embeddings tied to its unique intrinsic and
extrinsic properties, allowing a transformer to infer this relationship without
explicit geometric modeling. The architecture combines convolutional image
encoders for individual views with cross-view transformer layers to generate
semantic map representations. This approach yields efficient, real-time results
and achieves top performance on the nuScenes dataset with significantly improved
inference speeds.

The patterns of proteins within a cell regulate various critical functions including cell reproduction and movement, often involving significant changes in cell form. Such alterations to cell form can in turn influence the dynamics of pattern-forming proteins leading to an intricate interplay between cell shape and chemical changes. Despite extensive computational studies of this intricate dynamics, its underlying mechanisms are still poorly understood. In order to clarify some of these mechanisms, we have explored a conceptual framework of cellular polarity on a dynamic linear framework, drawing from differential geometry. We then derived equations governing chemical reactions on evolving curved surfaces and, by examining these equations mathematically, demonstrated that dynamic cell membrane shape can induce unstable patterns in some membrane areas referred to as local instabilities. Additionally, localized deformations of membrane geometry can (temporarily) suppress the emergence of patterns or even spatially reposition already existing patterns. We clarified the reasoning behind our findings by applying and extending the theory of local equilibria in systems with conservation of mass and diffusion. By using this theory, we discovered a simple criterion for identifying unstable patterns resulting from dynamic cell membrane geometry. The interplay between cell membrane shape deformations and reaction dynamics leads to an unexpected variety of patterns including oscillations, moving waves, and standing waves which wouldn't occur under constant cell membrane shape. Our study found that local cell membrane geometry influences cellular patterns in systems with conservation of mass.

In the field of natural language processing, euphemisms have surprisingly garnered little attention despite being integral to polite and creative expression. Investigating this aspect proves challenging due to variations in language and differing opinions among humans regarding what constitutes a euphemism. A crucial initial step is gathering and examining instances of euphemisms, for which we created a corpus featuring potentially euphemistic terms along with contextual examples from a global corpus. We also compiled a subset of texts showcasing the opposite usage, facilitating future development. Moreover, this work involves interpreting various analyses conducted on our corpus. Firstly, sentiment analysis on euphemistic texts reveals that the associated terms generally mitigate negative and insulting sentiments. Notably, there were cases of discrepancy during an annotation task, in which individuals were asked to label potentially euphemistic terms as euphemistic or not in a selection of text examples, leading us to attribute these differences to multiple factors, such as terminology prevalence.

This paper examines the generalized Hyers-Ulam stability of the reciprocal functional equation: $f(2x+y)+f\left(\frac{x+y}{2}\right) = \frac{2f(x)f(y)}{f(x)+f(y)} + \frac{2f(x+y)f(y-x)}{3f(y-x)-f(x+y)}$ in the context of non-Archimedean space through a direct method of investigation.

This study examines highly accurate three-dimensional surface recognition in complex hydrodynamics for unobstructed surface fluid dynamics using a novel approach. Initially, a geometric algorithm is formulated to boost precision of detecting surface fluid particles within intricate flows. It detects these particles by continuously scanning the area within a spherical region through a cone-shaped area where each particle is located, verifying that a given cone area is devoid of neighboring particles to confirm it as a surface fluid particle. Subsequently, a more efficient semi-geometric method is proposed, derived from the geometric algorithm to decrease computation costs, where first fluid particles are located using a position divergence technique, then these are further identified using the geometric algorithm as surface fluid particles. Finally, the efficacy and reliability of the suggested method are proven by testing it on several theoretical examples.

I investigated six novel tests of general relativity through observation. Firstly, I demonstrated that a massive black hole merger near the galactic center generates a gravitational wave pulse capable of altering the Earth's orbit around the Moon. This shift, although minor (a millimeter at most), is detectable using lunar ranging methods. Secondly, I established a universal upper limit on the energy flux emitted from cosmic sources based on their redshift. Next, I explored the feasibility of intergalactic travel by modified inertia at low accelerations in Modified Newtonian Dynamics (MOND). The implications suggest that, at certain speeds, intergalactic travel might become possible with efficient fuel usage. In another study, I revealed that MOND could be the source of the observed dipole of the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB). Further research indicated that the gravitational pull of the Milky-Way's satellite galaxies causes dark matter to tunnel out of those systems. Lastly, I discovered that a charged particle can maintain an accelerated state indefinitely by aligning its frequency with the phase of a gravitational wave propagating within a uniform magnetic field, resulting in potentially significant electromagnetic emissions near gravitational-wave sources.

The scalar partial amplitude $m_n(\mathbb{I},\mathbb{I})$ can be calculated as a single integral within the positive tropical Grassmannian, achieving Global Schwinger Parameterization. This research advances the theory further by introducing a universal method to compute all partial amplitudes $m_n(\alpha,\beta)$ through an iterative limiting process. This limiting process can also be applied to derive an integral representation for $\phi^4$ amplitudes, resulting in the replacement of indicator functions with Dirac delta functions whose support regions break down into $\textrm{C}_{n/2-1}$ areas, corresponding to the $q^{\rm th}$-Catalan number. Each area contributes to an amplitude equivalent to $m_{n/2+1}(\alpha,\mathbb{I})$. This research establishes a combinatorial interpretation of these regions using non-crossing chord diagrams and develops a universal formula for $\phi^4$ amplitudes using Lagrange inversion. It begins the investigation of $\phi^p$ theories, identifying that their regions are represented in non-crossing $(p-2)$-chord diagrams, mirroring the structure of Green functions derived from connected Green functions within the planar limit of $\Phi^{p-1}$ matrix models. This research also discusses possible connections to current constructions based on Stokes polytopes and accordiohedra.

We conduct a theoretical investigation of the spatial pattern resulting from the symmetrical four-wave mixing process caused by Gaussian light in a narrow two-level atomic sample. Our calculations consider the complete spatial and spectral properties of the relevant nonlinear coefficients responsible for the process. This yields two key findings. Firstly, the overall power of the incoming beams influences the cross-sectional distribution of the four-wave mixing signals upon exiting the medium as well as their unobstructed propagation. Secondly, the spectral properties of the medium impact the longitudinal distribution of both generated signals during unobstructed propagation. We propose that the former phenomenon is analogous to medium saturation at high-intensity areas, whereas the latter can be attributed to a nonlinear refractive index within the atomic sample. Notably, these effects can exhibit symmetry between the signals, with the introduction of asymmetries resulting from the differing detunings from resonance of the incoming fields.

A new strategy is developed to choose the most effective polarizability 
distribution for metasurface apertures designed to generate a target radiation 
pattern. Metasurface apertures comprise an array of subwavelength metamaterial 
elements that act as radiating, polarizable dipoles. Ideal polarizability 
distributions can be determined by applying a holographic approach to first 
calculate necessary aperture fields, and then applying equivalence principles to 
convert them to polarizability distributions. However, for practical, passive 
metamaterials, the phase and magnitude of polarizability are linked by their 
resonance properties. To address this constraint, we introduce a family of 
mappings to bridge the gap between ideal and feasible polarizability 
distributions, visualized by comparing their complex plane representations. 
Utilizing these mappings, optimal beam patterns can be achieved from 
metasurface antennas despite the limitations inherent in resonator properties. 
We present the technique, along with specific examples, and demonstrate the 
approach's effectiveness with numerical simulations.

Developing advanced surgical tools and workflow monitoring systems relies heavily on effective activity recognition in surgical videos. As surgeries are lengthy, unpredictable procedures, state-of-the-art models for surgical video analysis frequently employ a two-part approach using a backbone network and temporal modeling techniques. In this research, various cutting-edge backbones and temporal models were evaluated to determine which architecture results in the highest performance for surgical activity recognition tasks. Initial performance benchmarks were conducted using an extensive activity recognition dataset featuring over 800 surgery videos captured in multiple real-world operating rooms. Following that, the models' effectiveness was tested on two smaller, publicly accessible datasets, namely the Cholec80 and Cataract-101 datasets, which contained significantly fewer videos. It was found that the Swin-Transformer coupled with the BiGRU temporal model displayed superior performance across both datasets. Finally, the study explored the adaptability of this model by fine-tuning it on new datasets and experimenting with an innovative unsupervised domain adaptation method in a different hospital setting.

The latest CDF mass measurement of $W$, 80,433 $\pm$ 9 MeV, is a highly precise direct measurement. Yet, it significantly differs from the predicted mass by the Standard Model, which is 80,359.1 $\pm$ 5.2 MeV, with a discrepancy of $7\sigma$. In the CDF experiment, an outdated version of ResBos code was used, which only offers predictions at the NNLL+NLO accuracy level. The more recent ResBos2 code has the ability to produce calculations with the N${}^3$LL+NNLO precision. Our findings suggest that the CDF experiment predominantly utilized data-driven methods that encompass most of the higher order corrections, and implementing these corrections would at most result in a reduction of 10 MeV in the reported value.

This paper examines the issue of rectifying malfunctioning 3D objects by
emphasizing the significance of user interactions. Unlike prior research, which
focused on developing passive models that infer object functionality from static
objects, our approach considers the practical consequences of object interactions.
When encountering a faulty object, individuals use mental simulations to analyze
its properties and propose potential repairs. Motivated by this concept, we
introduce FixIt, a dataset consisting of approximately 5,000 inadequately
designed 3D physical objects along with suggested repair options. Our FixNet
framework replicates human thought processes by combining perception and
mechanical dynamics, comprising three core components: perception, physical
simulation, and functionality prediction. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that
our proposed framework outperforms control models significantly, while also
generalizing effectively to objects with analogous interaction types.

To improve our understanding of the Dirac CP-violating phase, we modify previous models by incorporating perturbations that alter tribimaximal or bimaximal mixing patterns. We apply simple rotations to these matrices, translate them into a standard format, and derive correlations between the Dirac CP-phase and neutrino oscillation angles. We then analyze these relations in conjunction with existing experimental data to identify potential CP-phase constraints and calculate its probability density. Additionally, we explore potential opportunities for future experiments and develop a model that combines A4 modular symmetry with the perturbed scenarios to match current oscillation parameters.

A novel method for estimating the acoustic transfer function (ATF) is presented. It addresses both the ATF's physical characteristics and regional orientations to achieve more accurate predictions. Unlike existing interpolation methods which primarily focus on receiver areas, the proposed approach can estimate ATFs for both source and receiver regions using a discrete set of measured ATF data. To enhance the accuracy of the method, a new kernel function is formulated by incorporating directional weights in the reproducing kernel Hilbert space. We also explore various optimization techniques to adjust the method's parameters. Computational tests reveal that incorporating directional weights improves the proposed method's performance.

We investigated the expected mass distributions in proton-proton collisions at various energies, including 13, 14, 27, 100, 300, and 500 TeV, which involve dijet resonances produced from excited quarks. Our research delved into both theoretical predictions from the generator and the observed experimental patterns to understand how different factors, including the excited quark's natural width, proton momentum distributions, radiation, and experimental resolution, contribute to the mass distributions. The findings presented a detailed examination of both the dijet mass distributions and the signal acceptance in specified mass windows, which centers on the dijet resonances. Our analysis showed that for a specific range of resonance masses, approximately between 10% and 50% of the collision energy, the dijet mass distributions exhibit a high degree of consistency across various collision energies, indicating that these patterns are largely unaffected by variations in resonance mass and collision energy. The outcome of our work provides valuable support to our previous study on the sensitivity of proton-proton colliders to detect dijet resonances presented during Snowmass 2021.

We present an unsupervised approach to a generative model for scenes that utilizes a mid-level representation, where scenes are broken down into groups of distinct spatial elements - 'blobs' of features, which are then arranged into a scene. This arrangement is facilitated through a differentiable grid and a generative adversarial network that converts it into a visible image. Due to the localized nature of blob placement, our model effectively identifies specific elements in a scene and their respective positions. This is showcased by our model's ability to manipulate objects in a scene without supervision, create new scenes based on specific constraints, and break down real-world images into individual components. Our method, BlobGAN, is tested on a challenging indoor scene dataset and achieves higher image quality than StyleGAN2 as measured by FID score. Further visual results and interactive demo are available on our project page: https://www.dave.ml/blobgan

Analyzing electrocardiogram signals by cardiologists can be a labor-intensive task that may soon be replaced by machine learning-based automated classification. However, applying Deep Learning in healthcare is limited by a lack of transparency, making it difficult to understand the underlying decision-making process. This study aimed to develop more transparent and interpretable deep learning models for classifying electrocardiogram rhythms, by creating and comparing the performance of Convolutional Neural Network and Long Short-Term Memory classifiers with shallower models. Various interpretability methods were employed to analyze the relationships between different variables across the dataset, including Partial Dependence Plots and Shapley Additive Explanations. Specifically, this research examined whether the interpretability of the Gradient Weighted Class Activation Maps (Grad-Cam) technique varies depending on the correctness of the classifications within each class. The classifiers were rigorously evaluated using cross-validation techniques and non-parametric statistical testing. The results revealed that Grad-Cam was the most effective technique for explaining the predictions of the proposed CNN and LSTM models, which generally focused on the QRS complex when making predictions.

A teaching model, called 'No-Clash Teaching' or 'NC-Teaching', was proposed, which offers optimal performance in a rigorous sense. It fulfills a key criterion of collusion-freeness and is outperformed only by itself in terms of the teaching dimension. It has been proven that the maximum number of concepts in a domain is significantly lower for the NC-Teaching model compared to other models with the same property. This paper presents three primary findings. Firstly, concept classes of NC-Teaching dimension one can be described by unique, graph-induced models called tournaments. Secondly, a specific family of concept classes exhibits a logarithmic growth in teaching dimension despite having an NC-Teaching dimension of one. Thirdly, the paper improves an existing upper bound on the maximum number of concepts in a domain by a significant margin using probabilistic methods and complex graph theory.

Dark matter is viewed as a gas consisting of massive particles that interact through gravity, undergo collisions, and transfer energy in quantized form. A new nonrelativistic quantum framework for this dark matter model has been formulated using an equation recently derived for neutral, particle particles. This theory clarifies the quantum phenomena exhibited by the particles, determines the specific wavelength of the energy quanta involved, imposes restrictions on the mass of the dark matter particles, and forecasts the presence of a measurable gravitational wave signature linked to dark matter halos.

The concept of an optical exciton - a pair of photo-excited electrons and holes within a crystal lattice - has been extensively used to analyze a wide range of phenomena in semiconductors, including the appearance of certain spectral signatures and predicted behaviors such as condensation, diffusion, and recombination. These phenomena are typically understood as resulting from the optical excitons acting as discrete, well-defined particles that are apparent in the linear absorption spectrum. In contrast, this paper presents an alternative perspective, based on many-body perturbation theory, that suggests that electron-phonon interactions cause optical excitons to decompose into simpler, "elemental" excitons, which are fundamentally different from optical excitons in that they lack the effects of induced electric fields. We demonstrate this idea through an examination of two real systems: monolayer MoS$_2$, where the lowest exciton is not optically active, and monolayer MoSe$_2$, where it is. By calculating exciton-phonon coupling matrix elements using first-principles methods, we show that one consequence of this decomposition is a homogeneous broadening of absorption peaks that even affects the lowest excitons. We further illustrate this point by computing exciton-phonon transition rates. Overall, our findings suggest that the optical excitons lose their structure as they transform into elemental excitons, which represent the genuine intrinsic excitations of the system, persisting long after external disturbances and induced fields have disappeared.

A relatively new method for integrating knowledge involves accepting multiple perspectives, allowing for reasoning with conflicting viewpoints rather than combining them.  A system for handling a variety of propositional standpoint logics, called nested sequent calculi, is presented in this paper - this is a proof method involving the manipulation of trees with formula collections as nodes.  An algorithm for automating standpoint reasoning with nested sequent calculi, using non-deterministic methods to search for valid proofs, is introduced, and it can efficiently determine validity with worst-case optimal performance by using a novel technique known as "coloring" in which formulas are assigned different "colors" to narrow down potential paths in proof search.  As a result, this method enables the evaluation of propositional standpoint formula validity within CoNP complexity.  It is also shown how valid input formulas can produce complete proofs and how certain cases can generate a counter-example (counter-model), which together act as clear explanations for both the correctness or the incorrectness of the formula being analyzed.

In the case of spin torque magnetic memories, electrical manipulation of spin currents facilitates magnetic bit switching. These systems usually comprise multiple layers including a ferromagnetic layer and one providing spin injection. Spin injection can be accomplished by layers displaying significant spin Hall effect, a phenomenon characterized by spin-orbit torque. In the current research, a magnetic bit exhibiting spin-orbit torque is successfully implemented in a singular two-dimensional system featuring intrinsic magnetism and substantial Berry curvature. By analyzing AB-stacked MoTe2/WSe2, a magnetic Chern insulator is discovered at a specific carrier density, corresponding to one hole per moire superlattice site. It was observed that switching the applied current causes a hysteretic change in the material's resistivity, and superconducting quantum interference device imaging revealed that this switching involves the reversal of magnetic domains in the material. Additionally, a correlation is observed between domain reversals and measured spin accumulation near the high-Berry curvature Hubbard band edges, which is consistent with spin-orbit torque acting within the material, a finding that can be applied to similar moire materials, including MoTe2/WSe2, and could potentially lead to an improvement in control over magnetic order through the use of significantly reduced current densities of 10^3 Amps per square centimeter compared to reported values for other systems.

Results have been compiled for the measurement of boosted top-quark pair production, specifically single, double, and triple-differential cross-sections. These cross-sections were recorded at a 13 teraelectronvolt energy level using the ATLAS detector. By monitoring the hadronic decay of top quarks as large-radius jets with high transverse momentum, and subsequently removing detector effects, particle-level cross-sections were determined. A cross-section value of approximately 331 was found, though this falls short of a prediction from Powheg+Pythia with a next-to-leading order accuracy, though this discrepancy is relatively insignificant within theoretical margins of error. By contrasting parton-level cross-sections, where effects of quark decay and parton showering have been discounted, against fixed-order calculations with a next-to-next-to-leading order accuracy, and comparing results to NNLO calculations, one can discern patterns and compare these results to various NLO models and NNLO calculations to see that the latter tend to have better overall agreements with collected data. By employing an analysis of a Standard Model using an effective field theory, one can establish and test limits on several four-fermion operator coefficients, specifically Wilson coefficients, and see that the differential cross-sections correlate generally in accordance with expectations from most next-order level models in the field.

In our research, we explore the process of quantum many-body teleportation, in which one qubit is transmitted via a complex quantum system following a scrambling transformation and limited local measurements. Contrary to typical protocols, which necessitate a double replication of the system along with reversed time evolution, our findings reveal that this can be achieved in a two-dimensional XY spin-1/2 model under more lenient constraints. The prerequisite long-range entanglement essential for successful teleportation originates from a distinctive property of this model, known as rainbow scars. To realize this entangled state, we propose an efficient method: by initiating with a product state, evolving it through successive measurements and feedback control, all while acting upon only two qubits.

Legged robots face difficulties replicating agile maneuvers like sprinting and rapid turns in uncontrolled environments. We have developed an advanced end-to-end controller that has broken records for agility with the MIT Mini Cheetah, allowing it to reach speeds of up to 3.9 meters per second while maintaining balance on diverse terrains like grass, ice, and gravel. This system exhibits exceptional stability when encountering disruptions. This neural network-based controller is initially trained through simulated reinforcement learning and then successfully transferred to real-world applications. It features two crucial components: (1) adaptive velocity-based learning pathways, and (2) an online terrain-adaptation strategy for seamless simulation-to-real environment transition. Visual demonstrations of the robot's abilities can be viewed here: https://agility.csail.mit.edu/

Digital health passes demonstrate an alternative approach to controlling COVID-19 outbreaks by validating quarantine and vaccination status in a legally compliant manner. However, existing DHP systems are hindered by region-based controls and centralized data storage, making them less adaptable to varying jurisdictional requirements and privacy standards. This work introduces a decentralized PHI storage and validation mechanism for DHPs using an updated two-stage handshake process integrated into a blockchain consensus algorithm. The proposed mechanism empowers individuals to universally validate their health status with any authority while safeguarding their PHI and personal autonomy. The implemented protocol exhibits stability in the face of potential cyber attacks and demonstrates its feasibility in simulations involving significant participant numbers.

Recent research on velocity discrepancies in widely spaced binary stars, measured using GAIA with high accuracy, presents a promising test for theories attempting to replicate dark matter. As binary stars should behave strictly according to Newtonian standards in traditional dark-matter models, MOND-like theories, on the other hand, generate significantly distinct predictions if certain observational obstacles are addressed. To this end, our updated investigation utilises GAIA EDR3 data, involving a selection of 73 159 potential wide binary stars within a 300 parsec radius and possessing G<17 magnitudes. Following component mass estimation based on a main-sequence mass-luminosity relationship, we investigate the distribution of relative velocity ratios in relation to circular orbit expectations versus projected separation. As was the case in previous studies, these distribution patterns consistently show a pronounced peak close to Newtonian predictions alongside a long 'tail' of significantly increased velocity ratios, potentially caused by hierarchical triple systems containing unseen stars. A mixture of simulated binary, triple, and flyby populations for both General Relativity (GR) and Modified Newtonian Dynamics (MOND) is then fitted against the observed distribution patterns, yielding standard gravity preference over a specific MOND implementation. Although the parameter space for triple systems and MOND variations has yet to be fully explored, refined data from upcoming GAIA releases, combined with detailed investigation of a subset of these binary systems, should ultimately allow binary stars to conclusively decide between GR and MOND.
This paper examines connections between the eigenvalues of Hermitian matrices and their diagonal entries.

Hypergraphs provide an effective means of representing high-order relationships among objects, with numerous real-world applications in data analysis. In this research, a novel heat diffusion process for hypergraphs is introduced, leading to the development of a polynomial-time algorithm capable of identifying bipartite components with approximations. We establish the efficacy of our proposed algorithm through both theoretical proof and experimental validation across a variety of hypergraph datasets, demonstrating superior performance compared to existing solutions.

The principle of entropy increase suggests that in physics, irreversible processes exist, particularly in systems that are isolated and cannot decrease in entropy. One example of an irreversible process is a normal metal's loss of electric current to heat due to resistance. However, in the case of a superconductor's transition to normal, the situation was initially perceived as irreversible before the discovery of the Meissner effect. If the superconducting transition is considered irreversible, the Meissner effect would contradict this, indicating the possibility of an inverse process. The idea that entropy cannot decrease forced physicists to reevaluate the superconducting transition, now understood as a phase transition after the Meissner effect. Unfortunately, the conventional theory of superconductivity, created within a reversible thermodynamic framework, still generates inconsistencies, predicting the production of Joule heat in an otherwise superconducting system. According to the conventional theory, the persistent current is destroyed upon entering the normal state but then spontaneously reappears as the superconducting state is re-established, in contradiction with the principle of entropy increase. The theory's success highlights doubts surrounding the validity of the principle of entropy increase.

A persistent increase in gamma-ray emission from VER J0521+211, a source observed by various telescopes in 2013-2014, showed a peak radiation intensity approximately 37% of the Crab Nebula's. Multispectral observations revealed a correlation between the X-ray and gamma-ray levels and that the X-ray emission grew stronger when the gamma-ray levels increased. Based on this and four different scenarios of the universe's cosmic light background, researchers set a limit of 0.31 or lower for the object's redshift with 95% confidence. Unlike the X-ray and gamma-ray bands, optical radiation didn't significantly increase during the observation period. Changes in optical to X-ray spectral levels may indicate the object's peak radiation frequency broadens during such periods. A model using a one-zone synchrotron self-Compton method could describe this change, suggesting that the object is an intermediate-frequency-peaked BL Lac object consistent with its spectral and jet radio morphological features.

Recent research has demonstrated the potential of differentiable physics for
solving soft-body manipulation tasks with great effectiveness. Nevertheless, 
a major challenge arises when using the standalone differentiable physics 
solver with suboptimal initial contact points or for multi-stage tasks 
involving multiple contact points. To overcome these obstacles, we introduce 
a novel contact point discovery approach called CPDeform, which integrates an 
optimal transport-based mechanism with the differentiable physics solver. This 
allows CPDeform to navigate through complex multi-stage tasks more efficiently, 
even when switching between different contact points is required. To assess the 
performance of our proposed approach, we introduce an updated version of 
PlasticineLab that includes a new benchmark consisting of seven intricate 
soft-body manipulation tasks, PlasticineLab-M. Extensive experiments confirm 
that CPDeform is capable of automatically discovering effective contact points, 
which can guide the differentiable physics solver to successfully complete tasks 
that the original solver cannot. Furthermore, CPDeform demonstrates 
performance that is either superior to or comparable with that achieved through 
expert-designed contact points.

A wide prevalence of excessive mixing is observed in lower-mass stars that have progressed to the upper giant branch phase. This phenomenon has commonly been attributed to thermohaline mixing. Existing one-dimensional stellar evolution models have been developed to account for thermohaline mixing, yet a lack of empirical evidence from observational data has limited the evaluation of various mixing prescriptions. In order to address this, a novel framework is introduced that enables the direct comparison of predicted trends from one-dimensional stellar evolution programs with observed levels of extra mixing. This method relies on nitrogen-to-carbon ratios measured by the SDSS-IV APOGEE survey, along with a reduced density ratio obtained from one-dimensional stellar evolution programs, and 3D fluid dynamics simulations to determine how the efficiency of mixing is influenced by reduced density ratios. It was discovered that the amount of extra mixing is closely tied to the reduced density ratio and the relationships between reduced density ratios and fundamental stellar parameters were shown to be consistent regardless of modeling choices. Additionally, an inverse correlation was found between the available data for mixing in the lower-mass stars that were analyzed, indicating a tendency towards lower reduced density ratios, thereby providing guidance for future modeling efforts. These results demonstrate an increase in mixing at low reduced density ratios, consistent with current theoretical hydrodynamic models for thermohaline mixing. This novel framework establishes a benchmark for future theoretical efforts, providing a method to validate the amount of extra mixing, as well as trends in mixing intensity versus fundamental stellar parameters.

We examine properties of two four-quark mesons, $X_0$ and $X_0^{\prime}$, possessing the diquark-antidiquark structure $[ud][\overline{c}\overline{s}]$ and having a spin-parity of $0^{+}$. We investigate the possibility of these states matching the $X_0(2900)$ resonance identified by the LHCb collaboration, through modeling them as tetraquarks formed by combining either axial-vector or scalar diquarks with antidiquarks. Using the QCD two-point sum rule method and taking into account condensates of up to dimension 15, we calculate the spectroscopic parameters for both $X_0$ and $X_0^{\prime}$. We compute partial widths for their decays into $DK$ pairs, as well as estimate the full widths for the $X_0^{(\prime)}$ states. This is achieved by determining the strong couplings at the $X_0^{(\prime)}DK$ vertices using the light-cone sum rule method and soft-meson approximation, providing results for their masses, $m=(2545\pm 160)$ MeV and $m^{\prime}=(3320 \pm 120)$ MeV. However, the obtained values, along with predicted full widths $\Gamma_{0}=(140 \pm 29)$ MeV and $\Gamma_{0}^{\prime}=(110 \pm 25)$ MeV, suggest that neither state corresponds to the $X_0(2900)$ resonance, instead providing essential information for future research on the diquark-antidiquark structures $X_0$ and $X_0^{\prime}$.

Among future ground-based gravitational-wave detectors planned for the 2030s, the Einstein Telescope stands out due to its ability to generate a null stream, a type of signal-free data combination, that can facilitate previously inaccessible noise model tests. This detector's null stream and its associated analysis challenges are crucial to understanding how they will affect the overall performance of the Einstein Telescope. Our analysis shows that this unique feature enables effective transient detector glitch elimination and aids current gravitational-wave searches. Importantly, the techniques discussed here are highly efficient in computational terms and don't rely on prior knowledge about specific glitch models. Furthermore, the null stream allows unbiased noise power spectrum estimation even when dealing with multiple loud signals, both during online data analysis and post-analysis offline processing. Other approaches to utilizing this capability in the Einstein Telescope and related networks will also be explored. Lastly, the study identifies limitations of the null-stream analysis for the Einstein Telescope as well as potential challenges that might arise when analyzing data from multiple detectors.

Current low-mass red giant models fail to replicate the position of the luminosity bump on the red giant branch, a feature related to the convective envelope during the first dredge-up phase. Nevertheless, employing a treatment of convective overshoot beneath the envelope allows for better matching of model luminosity bumps to observed values, according to the global seismic parameters measured for red giants. Nonetheless, individual stars cannot be analyzed through these parameters. Since the interior structure, particularly around the convective boundary, holds critical information about the interior, red giant mixed modes are used to investigate interior processes, such as overshoot. Through a grid of models differing in mass, metal content, surface gravity, and the description of overshoot beneath the convective zone, alterations to the overshoot amplitude and its prescription in low-mass stellar models reveal distinct changes in the frequencies of their dipole mixed modes and in average mixed mode period spacings and gravity mode phase offsets.

Active visual working memory enables us to mentally store and manipulate the images around us. Despite a lack of clarity surrounding its neural mechanisms, research into contralateral delay activity - an electrical signal found over the brain region opposite to the remembered image - has provided insight into visual working memory processes. To verify its validity, eight prior studies utilizing EEG data to analyze contralateral delay activity were re-examined using a uniform method and publicly available data. Our replication of all eight studies successfully yielded consistent results and highlighted the effectiveness of using a basic EEG analysis pipeline in isolating this activity. We draw attention to trends that emerged and raise questions about how CDA changes over time, as well as its presence during the retrieval stage, a gap in prior research that our study sought to address. We also offer recommendations for researchers seeking to reproduce similar studies, having encountered our own set of challenges along the way.

For every connected complex subvariety, we find a pseudoconvex region that allows every bounded holomorphic function on it to be isometrically extended. Our proof also addresses a specific case of two intersecting analytic disks; it states that for it to extend every bounded holomorphic function, every matrix-valued function would also need to extend isometrically. However, under specific circumstances, notably when $\Omega$ is the symmetrized bidisk, we can demonstrate a contradiction, by finding a linear isometric extension for functions vanishing at a point, indicating an impossibility.

New sensing capabilities are provided by nanomechanical resonators made from van der Waals materials, specifically for measuring absorbed laser energy. The resonant frequency shifts of these resonators, resulting from light absorption, can be enhanced by integrating them into a specific interferometer structure. However, the dependence of this enhancement on the movement of the resonator has yet to be thoroughly examined. In an effort to address this gap, we have been studying a specific type of van der Waals resonator fabricated using niobium diselenide, with a focus on highly reflective substrates and driven by electrical means. Our findings can be described using an absorptive heating model facilitated by a specific interferometer structure. According to this model, the measurable response to laser light varies across different types of van der Waals drum-type resonators, including drumheads composed of niobium diselenide at specific thickness levels, yielding higher performance compared to analogous structures. Our detailed examination of this phenomenon further demonstrates that niobium diselenide resonator performance, including sensitivity and tuning range, scales directly with material thickness, thus enabling a framework for designing displacement-based thermal sensors utilizing the described setup.

Deep learning change detection methods rely heavily on annotated data for optimal performance. Annotating remote sensing images is a labor-intensive and costly process, but large volumes of unlabeled data are becoming increasingly available. To bridge this gap, a novel semi-supervised change detection model is proposed. By incorporating an unsupervised change detection loss in addition to a cross-entropy loss, the model leverages information from unlabeled image pairs. It does this by ensuring the consistency of the change probability map when small perturbations are applied to the deep feature differences. Experiment results demonstrate that this approach can match the performance of supervised methods with as little as 10% of the labeled training data.

This paper outlines an experiment using our randomized hints method to help a theorem prover, OTTER, derive Axiom(5) from the initial axioms (1 through 4) in Infinite-Valued Lukasiewicz Logic through a process involving guided search and resolution. The experiment generated a series of 900 hints sets, ranging in size from 30 to 60 items, to facilitate OTTER's search for a solution. By evaluating the performance of these sets, we identified the optimal set of 30 hints and observed an unexpected spike in the number of generated clauses resulting from applying our randomized hints strategy.

A spiral galaxy's spiral pattern can be discerned using various observational markers like dust in the interstellar space, electrons in ionized zones, molecular gas, or atomic hydrogen in specific regions. This work employs a simulated model combining magnetic fluid dynamics (MHD) with particle motion to examine spiral pattern development and gas-driven star formation within a galactic disk. We address several inquiries, such as: How do galaxies appear distinct when viewed through various gas attributes? Do a galaxy's spiral features change based on the attribute used to detect them? Do the simulation's spiral arms vary in shape and width depending on the attribute observed? Is it possible to create a model to accurately measure arm width? Furthermore, is this model applicable to all gas attributes? To resolve these questions, we have developed a technique for detecting and extracting spiral structures in a galactic disk. Utilizing this method, we investigated how the spiral pattern manifests across diverse gas attributes, with a particular focus on star formation behavior and how it interacts with the spiral pattern along and across it.

Galaxies hosting AGN with distorted radio jets are utilized as markers for densely populated galaxy environments like groups and clusters. This practice is predicated on the idea that the jets are warped by the resistance from a gas-rich medium that the host galaxy navigates. However, a significant portion of AGN residing in these environments display undistorted jets, prompting an investigation into why some are profoundly impacted by their surroundings while others remain relatively unaffected. We have conducted an environmental study on 185 AGN featuring distorted jets and 191 AGN featuring non-distorted jets by identifying neighboring galaxies utilizing an algorithm known as 'Friends-of-Friends'. The analysis indicates that AGN possessing distorted jets tend to reside in groupings and clusters, whereas those AGN possessing non-distorted jets prefer to inhabit solitary galaxies or galaxy pairs. A more detailed examination reveals that AGN possessing distorted jets prefer to reside in larger, more galaxy-dense groupings when confined to groupings consisting of three or more galaxies. Conversely, non-distorted AGN have a greater propensity to reside in groupings where they are the brightest central galaxy. Our study also found that galaxy groupings containing AGN featuring distorted jets possess greater galaxy density than those groupings containing AGN featuring non-distorted jets. A curious observation suggests that a population of AGN possessing distorted jets exist within what appear to be less densely populated regions, indicating they may be embedded within cosmic filaments. Our overall findings imply that AGN possessing distorted jets prefer to reside in larger, more densely populated and less stable environments, establishing a link between a galaxy's radio structure and its environment.

This study develops a model for capturing the intricacies of conversation, 
specifically listener movements in response to a speaker: using multimodal inputs 
from the speaker, our model can generate various potential listener responses.
Our framework incorporates both audio and motion inputs from the speaker via 
a motion-audio cross transformer and introduces a novel, probabilistic approach 
to model realistic listener movements through a motion-encoding variational 
autoencoder. As a result, our method organically replicates the nuances of 
interactive conversations, while also generating authentic, synchronous 3D 
listener facial movements (as seen in our accompanying video). Our experiments 
demonstrate our method's superior performance, both qualitatively and 
quantitatively, over existing methods. Additionally, to facilitate further 
research in this area, we introduce a substantial, publicly available dataset 
featuring real-world conversations, along with accompanying code and video 
demonstrations, available at https://evonneng.github.io/learning2listen/.

Recent high-performance optical flow models often utilize finite-step recurrent updates, emulating established algorithms to refine their flow estimation iteratively. Nonetheless, these RNNs result in excessive computation and memory consumption, with unstable convergence leading to performance declines. To address these drawbacks, we introduce deep equilibrium flow estimators, which directly find stable flow estimation by leveraging an infinite-level implicit layer. This method requires minimal training memory and isn't limited to specific model types, allowing its application to diverse flow estimation models. Using deep equilibrium estimators facilitates faster flow computations and requires 4 to 6 times less training memory than their RNN counterparts, yielding better results at equal computational budgets. Moreover, we present a novel sparse fixed-point correction scheme to enhance the stability of deep equilibrium models. Evaluations across real-world scenarios reveal our method surpasses existing state-of-the-art approaches in the Sintel and KITTI datasets with significant efficiency gains in computation and memory.

This paper examines two variants of a multi-dimensional opinion dynamics model proposed by HK. These two models capture how individuals adjust their opinions across multiple subjects, based on their peer influence. The distinguishing factor between the two models lies in how individuals select influencers. For one model, agents compare their aggregate opinions and engage with those whose views align within a specified margin of error. An alternative proof of this model's convergence properties shows that individual opinions converge to a single value or distinct groups only when the averages of these opinions do the same. In the other model, agents compare individual opinions and influence one another if their opinions on each topic do not differ excessively. Conditions under which this model exhibits order-preservation across topics have been identified, and a proof demonstrates that the global spread of opinions does not increase over time.

Recent studies have demonstrated that motion planning efficiency can be significantly enhanced by retrieving and learning from past experiences stored in a database. Most existing works utilize basic similarity measures, which restrict their performance to specific data sets. To address this shortcoming, we propose a new framework, FIRE, which extracts essential representations of planning problems and develops an adaptive similarity measure based on these elements. To create a training dataset, we introduce a unique self-supervised technique that automatically identifies analogous and dissimilar patterns within existing solution paths. A Siamese network is then trained with this contrastive data, leading to a learned similarity function embedded within its latent space. FIRE was tested on an eight-degree-of-freedom robot with diverse motion planning tasks in five categories, featuring sensed environments. Our results reveal that FIRE successfully retrieves pertinent experiences to inform and optimize sampling-based planners even in situations beyond its initial training, thereby outperforming other comparative benchmarks.

Accurate, real-time population information is vital for making informed decisions in areas like city planning, disaster response, and effectively allocating public services. To achieve this, precise demographic data is crucial. Conventional census methods are costly and labor-intensive. Advances in statistics and machine learning have led to new population estimation techniques, which, however, often rely on limited, private datasets. As a result, testing and refining these methods is difficult. We address this issue by introducing a large, publicly accessible dataset of population estimation in 98 European cities. The comprehensive dataset integrates data on terrain elevation, climate, land usage, night lighting, and high-resolution satellite imagery, along with mapping data from the Open Street Map project. We anticipate that our contribution will significantly benefit researchers in developing advanced population estimation methodologies.

A major research area in audio processing focuses on automatically generating informative descriptions of audio segments. Most current methods extract sound attributes from audio files and input them into models based on encoder-decoder and transformer designs to produce captions. Due to limited data and limitations in these architectures' learning capabilities, additional data is needed, particularly sound attributes, to generate more natural and coherent descriptions. To tackle these issues, a new model based on encoder-decoder design is introduced that incorporates not only sound attributes but also event labels extracted from the audio. Utilizing pre-trained sound attributes and event detection methods, numerous experiments were conducted with varied input combinations to determine their effectiveness on the task of automatically captioning audio. These extensive experiments conducted across multiple datasets showed that combining event labels with sound attributes leads to improved performance, and the proposed method surpasses or at least rivals current state-of-the-art models.

Human cognition combines linguistic and sensory inputs simultaneously to process language, and uniquely allows us to create novel abstract and tangible concepts. This ability to involve practical knowledge is crucial for solving problems under limited resources. Yet, existing NLU approaches largely focus on textual signals, failing to simulate human imagination capabilities, which impede models' ability to infer and learn effectively from small data sets. To overcome this, we present the Imagination-Augmented Cross-modal Encoder (iACE), offering a new perspective on NLU through imagination-enriched cross-modal understanding. iACE enhances visual imagination through external knowledge transfer from highly advanced pre-trained vision-and-language models. Empirical evaluations on GLUE and SWAG demonstrate that iACE outperforms visually-supervised pre-trained models, and the findings from few-shot settings validate the efficacy of iACE in resource-scarce NLU situations.

Building on conjectures by Spohn from 1991 and Jensen-Yau from 1999, recent studies on hydrodynamic limits in large-scale stochastic interacting particle systems have shown limited progress since the last few decades. This paper addresses the gap by proposing a general approach for applying the Boltzmann-Gibbs principle to a wide variety of non-steady-state and non-integrable particle interaction systems. A notable aspect of our method is its reliance on local dynamics, which makes it more versatile and applicable than previous methods that relied on global assumptions about system measures. A direct application of our method results in the derivation of the KPZ equation, which arises as a large-scale limit of height functions for a non-steady-state and non-integrable exclusion process with variable environment asymmetry. This outcome provides a response to a prominent question regarding the KPZ equation, and it sheds light on similar systems of interest in the broader field.

Gravitational waves, a natural consequence of Einstein's theory of general relativity, were first theorized by Einstein in 1915. The possibility of their existence had long been debated, as the initial linearized derivation did not fully account for the nuances of the theory. In 1960, scientists proved that gravitational waves are a solution to Einstein's equations under certain conditions. While much has been achieved, a definitive proof remains elusive, especially when accounting for the cosmological constant observed in our current understanding of the universe. This research takes inspiration from a previous model and introduces a novel method, which employs a geometry-based approach, eliminating ambiguities between coordinates and metrics. Using spherical triangles and geodesics, we establish a relationship between curvature fields and geodesic flow bundles, allowing us to calculate geodesics up to second order. This paper presents the initial step of solving the spatial component, which reduces a high-dimensional problem to a manageable 2D triangulation problem.

Studies of chiral and superconducting gaps were conducted in a four-fermion model where the interaction between fermions occurs in a two-dimensional plane. Research considered the influence of the angle at which mass is added to the massless Dirac cone and the chemical potential, which is non-zero in this model. Key results suggest that different behavior can be exhibited by systems in this model, which is characterized by planar fermions. When the effective tilt of the mass added to the massless Dirac cone is less than a certain critical value of about 0.55, and the superconducting coupling is negative, the superconducting phase remains stable. When the superconducting coupling is positive and the effective tilt of the mass added to the massless Dirac cone is less than this critical value, it's observed that the superconducting gap, which is caused by chemical potential, can exist as it does in similar graphene-like systems. When the effective tilt of the mass added to the massless Dirac cone exceeds the critical value of about 0.55 and the superconducting coupling is positive, it's observed that the superconducting phase can exist but within a more limited phase space. Lastly, analysis shows that when the superconducting coupling is positive, adding chemical potential suppresses the superconducting gap, making the manifestation of the metallic phase more favorable.

The appearance of power laws in various phenomena including matter transitions and language frequencies becomes more apparent when data sets become extensive. Research into power laws in neural data is gaining traction as larger datasets become available, leading researchers to attempt to characterise and apply frameworks such as Bayesian interpolation for data analysis. We explore these methods on synthetic and experimental data to identify their limitations. The analysis indicates that best-fit values for the parameters and corresponding uncertainty heavily depend on assumptions made in the noise model, chosen data ranges and particular recordings used. These findings question the reliability of making definitive statements regarding the exponents of power laws, while the conclusions drawn about the smoothness of population response in response to certain stimuli are not undermined, albeit the analysis for more complex stimuli raises doubts. We propose that a Bayesian interpolation approach may be a valuable framework for examining power laws in neural data that future research can adapt as needed.

A set of subspaces in a vector space $\mathbb{F}^n_q$ is called a subspace code, which does not contain the zero vector. A specific class of linear codes, referred to as LCD codes, have the property that their intersection with their duals is the zero vector. In this research, the concept of LCD subspace codes is presented, which can simplify the process of decoding such codes. Additionally, under certain circumstances, the use of equitable partitions from association schemes generates LCD subspace codes, as exemplified through instances in distance-regular graphs.

We calculate the full electroweak radiative corrections of order alpha to 9 Higgs boson production with the ILC at specific beam polarization settings, leveraging GRACE-Loop to achieve this calculation. By contrasting our result with the effects of factorized initial state radiation, we assess the significance of weak interactions in this context and conclude they must be factored in for precise Higgs boson measurements at ILC facilities.

A cutting-edge forecasting approach called PIDD-CG, which blends data-driven insights with mathematical physics, is designed to forecast how the probabilities of complex systems behave over time, even with limited information. By merging a high-efficiency method for processing vast amounts of data with a specialized statistical model that divides data into subcategories, PIDD-CG circumvents a major problem with analyzing high-dimensional systems. Within this approach, PIDD-CG uses a mix of established physical formulas and neural networks to replicate each subcategory, where neural networks are refined by a specific metric that closely matches turbulent systems' intense fluctuations. Ultimately, PIDD-CG accurately predicts the probabilities of highly unpredictable systems, which frequently exhibit random variations, sudden changes, and extreme events.

This paper develops a mathematical framework to represent the dynamics of Transactive Memory Systems, which are integral to collaborative task learning. Our model integrates factors at the individual level of expertise with the complex interactions between cooperative team members. Simulation results demonstrate that if all group members are non-resistant, they collectively achieve expertise equivalent to the most skilled individuals, reaching a state of proficiency as a cohesive unit. Conversely, if all group members are uncooperative, task transmission is contingent on the connectivity properties of the underlying network.

In the rapidly evolving landscape of computing, Artificial Intelligence and data processing are moving toward integration with the Internet of Things and Edge computing. For this convergence to succeed, it is essential to assess the capabilities of devices limited by resources. Among various devices used in these setups, Single-Board Computers offer a cost-effective, multi-purpose solution. Despite studies that have evaluated their performance under specific application conditions, there is a need for benchmarks that cater to Edge-based AI applications in network management and individual component performance evaluation. In this context, this study presents a new, comprehensive benchmarking tool, called LwHBench, which systematically measures the capabilities of Single-Board Computers, specifically taking into account their hardware constraints. LwHBench has been specifically designed for Raspberry Pi devices and has undergone an extensive evaluation on 45 devices for a continuous 100 days, providing a valuable dataset that AI techniques can utilize for device management. Furthermore, this dataset has been applied to various real-world scenarios to illustrate its versatility, including AI-enabled identification of devices and the assessment of their performance under varying conditions. Lastly, this tool has also been applied to a specific use case involving agriculture-focused devices.

This work examines the long-term transformation of Venus's atmosphere and its composition, shaped by an intricate exchange between the planet's interior and exterior. Despite the extensive research on the atmosphere's formation and evolution, many questions remain, requiring an interdisciplinary approach. We investigate various mechanisms contributing to the atmosphere's evolution, commencing with the origins and destinations of volatile elements. Starting from the planet's interior and progressing to the atmosphere, we discuss the processes of volcanic outbursts, surface-atmosphere interactions, and atmospheric loss. Furthermore, we delve into more intricate aspects of Venus's past, encompassing the effects of Late Accretion impacts, the link between magnetic field generation and long-term evolution, and the atmospheric consequences of geochemical and geodynamical feedback loops. We propose potential evolutionary paths that Venus may have followed from its formation to the present day, grounded in models and observations. Three hypothetical scenarios are explored: one in which atmospheric loss led to a desiccated Venus during its magma ocean phase, another in which Venus had long periods of surface liquid water followed by a catastrophic transition into a runaway greenhouse effect, and a third where inefficient outgassing led to the entrapment of hydrogen in the core and mantle oxidation. We discuss current knowledge and future research opportunities and missions necessary to enhance our comprehension of Venus's past, the intricate relationships between its interior, surface, and atmosphere, and the processes that have been operating in the planet's past, present, or future.

This work examines some lesser-known findings about marginal log-linear models, developing new results and highlighting their applicability in mediation analysis within logistic regression. Specifically, we investigate the connection between interaction parameters across distinct marginal distributions and present a method for estimating the same parameters across different marginals.
